Where the first one is clearly the same as one of the reported aspect ratios.  If it is used this
parameter needs to be very carefully defined along with the method calculation of the ellipse
parameters.

Circularity can also be measured and reported, but as this requires the measurement of the
grain perimeter, the effect of the map step/pixel size can alter the calculation significantly so
comparisons can only be made between maps of a similar step size.

3.4 Summary

    •     If measurements are to be taken from a map, ensure that it covers sufficiently large
        an area, especially in the case of elongated grains
    •   For large area/low magnification maps, consider stitching smaller areas acquired at
         higher magnifications to avoid edge distortions
    •   For many AM structures, use of a weighted average will give more consistent results
         with less dependence on the effect of step size and map quality
    •   Cumulative distribution graphs may illustrate differences between materials more
          clearly than histograms
    •   Parameters such as Feret Diameters, Linear Intercept or Ellipse fitted axes may give
       more useful information for non-equiaxed grains. However:
    •   Ensure the definition used to measure the parameter is known, or at a minimum the
         software used is reported to enable comparisons.

Having established some of the characteristic parameters of AM microstructures that can be
quantified and averaged over an entire map or sample, it is also worth considering how best to
understand the uniformity or otherwise of these parameters across a large region. AM
microstructures are determined by the melting of the powder layers and subsequent
solidification. Local variations in heat flow caused by changes in geometry, powder layer
deposition or input power and scan patterns can therefore lead to local variations in
solidification rates and thus microstructure.

EBSD (Electron Backscatter Diffraction) is employed to systematically investigate the influence of microstructure on fatigue crack initiation and propagation in Ti-6Al-4V. The crystallographic orientation, measured via EBSD, determines crack initiation sites, which occur on prismatic slip planes with high Schmid factors in both primary α grains and lamellar colonies. The Schmid factor quantifies the plastic strain activity and helps predict which slip systems are activated. At grain boundaries, crack deflection is governed by two competing factors: the geometric compatibility factor (strain compatibility at the interface) and the Schmid factor in neighboring grains. The elastic anisotropy of grains influences which factor dominates crack propagation—either high Schmid factor slip systems or high geometric compatibility factor slip systems. EBSD analysis, combined with KAM (Kernel Average Misorientation) mapping, reveals that crack paths remain planar and crystallographic, driven by mode II shear mechanisms, and are sensitive to microstructural features including grain size and orientation relationships.

The five-parameter grain boundary character distribution (GBCD) characterizes olivine grain boundaries using five parameters: three parameters describing disorientation (axis and angle) and two parameters describing grain boundary plane distribution (GBPD)—one radial and one azimuthal angle (Φ and θ). Recent EBSD technology enables statistical extraction of these parameters across large datasets (10^4-10^5 grain boundaries). The GBCD encompasses grain boundary geometry-energy relationships: particular grain boundary plane orientations at constant disorientation angles are more energetically favorable than others. Grain boundary energy minimization is primarily controlled by surface energy reduction of individual grains in contact rather than adaptation of special atomic configurations. Two main 3D EBSD measurement approaches exist: serial sectioning and stereological analysis of 2D orientation maps, though stereology requires materials without significant orientation texture.

## pqac-00000045

From text 'haines2025onthemartensitic pages 1-3'.

Michael P. Haines, Ehsan Farabi, Nima Haghdadi, and Sophie Primig. On the martensitic phase transformation and grain boundary character evolution in laser powder bed fusion 17-4 precipitation hardened stainless steel. Journal of Materials Science, 60:3430-3453, Jan 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-025-10645-8, doi:10.1007/s10853-025-10645-8. This article has 8 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt establishes that parent austenite grain size (PAGS) is directly linked to the resulting martensite microstructure in laser powder bed fusion 17-4 steel. Smaller PAGS improves grain boundary connectivity and increases length fractions of specific intervariant boundaries: 60°/[111] and 10.5°/[011]. The character of martensitic interfaces and martensite packet size significantly influence multiple material properties including toughness, strength, intergranular corrosion, cracking, and impurity segregation. The five-parameter characterization of interfaces reveals how PAGS controls both packet size and intervariant selection in martensite grains. The authors demonstrate that refined martensite microstructures improve the grain boundary network and selection of desirable intervariants, which is expected to impact toughness, strength, intergranular corrosion resistance, cracking behavior, and slip characteristics.

## pqac-00000046

From text 'haines2025onthemartensitic pages 21-23'.

Michael P. Haines, Ehsan Farabi, Nima Haghdadi, and Sophie Primig. On the martensitic phase transformation and grain boundary character evolution in laser powder bed fusion 17-4 precipitation hardened stainless steel. Journal of Materials Science, 60:3430-3453, Jan 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-025-10645-8, doi:10.1007/s10853-025-10645-8. This article has 8 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt contains references to multiple studies examining relationships between grain boundary characteristics and material properties in martensitic steels. Key topics include: parent austenite grain size effects on variant selection and intervariant boundary networks in lath martensite; the influence of austenite grain size on transformation behavior and mechanical properties; variant selection mechanisms at prior austenite grain boundaries and their micro-mechanical implications; and the distribution of internal interfaces in polycrystalline materials. The references also address microstructure dependence of impact toughness in duplex stainless steels and pitting corrosion behavior in laser powder bed fusion-produced duplex stainless steel. Additionally, grain refinement effects on thermal stability of metastable austenitic steel are discussed. These studies collectively suggest that prior austenite grain size, grain boundary character distribution, and intervariant boundary networks significantly influence both mechanical properties like toughness and corrosion resistance in martensitic and duplex stainless steels.

Journal of Materials Science, 60:3430-3453, Jan 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10853-025-10645-8, doi:10.1007/s10853-025-10645-8. This article has 8 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt discusses how grain boundary characteristics influence martensite properties in laser powder bed fusion 17-4 PH steel. The {110} boundary planes are identified as beneficial for controlling hydrogen embrittlement and dislocation plasticity. Intervariant boundary populations are sensitive to multiple factors including chemical composition, phase transformation mechanisms, crystallographic texture, temperature, strain, and grain size. Prior austenite grain size (PAGS) significantly affects martensite properties by altering the martensite start and finish temperatures. Smaller parent austenite grains (approximately 10.2 µm diameter in High N builds) suppress the martensite start temperature, while larger grains (52.6 µm in Low N builds) show different behavior. The martensitic microstructures preferentially develop {110} twist plane orientations, which aligns with observations in wrought martensitic steels. However, the excerpt does not specifically address five-parameter grain boundary distributions or detailed relationships between specific intervariant boundaries and corrosion resistance.

## 1. mingard2023theuseof pages 8-15 (Context ID: pqac-00000051)

Even without quantification, EBSD maps can help with visualisation of the processes going on
during manufacture, but this still necessitates an understanding of how best to plot maps and
choose the correct parameters and scales with which to produce the maps, or figures to
illustrate preferred crystal orientations. The wrong choice of EBSD acquisition conditions or
parameters to plot can result in erroneous conclusions, based on noisy or restricted and
therefore unrepresentative data sets.

This guide covers some of the basic aspects to consider when using EBSD to map an AM
sample. Firstly, it aims to illustrate some of the range of information that can be derived from
EBSD maps, and secondly and most importantly aims to ensure the data acquired is quantified
and reported in a manner that allows comparison with other EBSD datasets. Modern
commercially available EBSD software can generate maps and data very simply, but if the
details are not considered for how the software makes and reports measurements, invalid
comparisons can result. This can occur, for example, because different software programs use
different definitions for calculation of the value of a particular parameter, or because default
parameters are changed without realising, or frequently because the map colour scale is not
defined fully.





                                       Page 2 of 35The guide is aimed more at producers and users of AM materials or students relatively new to
the subject with limited familiarity with the operation of EBSD systems.  It is not a guide to
sample preparation or operation of EBSD systems, apart from where the operation impinges
on acquiring a useful dataset that is sufficiently representative to answer the questions being
asked about the process or sample. For more general information on the use of EBSD there
are a range of introductions to the technique including EBSD system suppliers websites,
YouTube videos [8] or published texts [9].

The range of AM materials and production conditions is extremely large, so the guide cannot
be fully comprehensive for every material type, so it concentrates on one of the alloy types,
Ni-base superalloys, which is a commonly produced material that is representative of many of
the issues encountered.





                                       Page 3 of 35This page was intentionally left blank





            Page 4 of 35                        Chapter 2

                Preferred orientations and
                 relationships to sample
              geometry





2  Preferred orientations and relationships to sample
   geometry





                                       Page 5 of 352.1 Sample location and definition

The majority of AM materials are produced by deposition of powder layers and progressive/
repeated sintering or melting of these layers between deposition by, for example, scanned
laser or electron beams. Therefore, in general the resulting microstructure will show a strong
relationship to the growth (Z) direction, perpendicular to the layers, and potentially also in the
orthogonal XY plane where X and Y are defined either by the sample geometry or the scan
pattern of the beam and its relationship to the sample geometry.

It is essential therefore that preparation of samples for polishing and EBSD examination can be
related to the three axes. This is often overlooked when samples are prepared from
components with a circular cross section (Figure 1).  If the axis of such a sample is in the
growth (Z) direction, the X-Y scan orientation can be lost if this is not noted before removal
from the AM machine. Figure 2 shows an example map of an X-Y plane in which there is clear
alignment of many of the grains, but it was not recorded how the axes the alignment might
define relate to the equipment axes or to the scan profile. Alternatively, if a cylinder (such as a
tensile specimen) is grown, or machined from a sample grown with the axis parallel to the
powder bed, the orientation of Z relative to a cross section may also be lost.  If the original
sintered surface is retained, the axes may be deduced from the surface appearance.



  a)                                b)                                 c)





Figure 1. a) As-built AM structures to produce cylinders for tensile testing parallel and perpendicular to the
  growth direction Z. b) Parallel growth cylinder removed from base and machined in o.d. with no obvious
    relationship to original X and Y or beam scan axis. c) Similarly cylinder machined from perpendicular
                growth direction with no obvious orientation relationship to X-z axes.





                                       Page 6 of 35Figure 2. IPF(z) orientation map of a section perpendicular to the Z growth direction of cylindrical sample of
  a Ni superalloy in which the orientation relative to the AM X and Y axes has been lost, so the repeating
                               structure cannot be related to the scan used.

2.2 Texture – crystallographic orientations relative to
    growth directions

The crystallographic texture, or preferred orientation, of a material affects its anisotropic
properties, including stiffness, mechanical strength, and electrical resistivity. In AM
manufactured materials, texture depends on the build axes and can be controlled by tuning
the build parameters.

2.2.1  Sample- microscope orientation relationships

Even if the relationship between the AM manufacturing X-Y-Z axes and the cross-section
polished for EBSD are known, a further alignment of axes needs to be understood when the
EBSD map is acquired. Figure 3a shows a map of Ni superalloy in which the grain elongation
clearly indicates the AM Z axis growth direction is vertical, but whether it is upwards or
downwards is less obvious. Depending on the relationship between the SEM sample tilt axis,
scanning axes and EBSD detector, the “top” of the sample when tilted may appear at the
bottom of the map(or even rotated 90° in some microscopes). Figures 3b and c show this
schematically for a cross section taken from the horizontal semi-cylindrical sample shown in
Figure 1a in which the tilted sample appears mapped upside down. A calibration method to
determine the relationship between sample, microscope and EBSD system axes may be found
in [10].

The relationship between the SEM-EBSD axes and the sample becomes even more important
when texture is to be analysed.





                                       Page 7 of 35  a)                         b)                                              c)





Figure 3. a) example of an IPF(z) orientation map of a section from a sample in which it is not obvious if the
 AM (Z) growth direction was up or down. b) Orientation of a sample in the SEM relative to the electron
         beam and EBSD camera and c) the map that could result from the orientation in b).

2.2.2  Sample Texture – orientation colour scale maps

The maps in Figures 3a and 3c use what is often the default orientation colour scale based on
an inverse pole figure, in which the colour is determined by the crystallographic direction or
plane normal to the plane of the mapped surface. For the illustrated case of a material with
cubic symmetry, the orientations will all fall within the portion of the stereographic projection
shown. Depending on the software used, this colour scale normal to the plane may be
referred to as IPF(z) or IPF[001], the former potentially confusing for AM as this EBSD Z axis
may well not be the same as the AM growth direction.

If only the default IPF scale is used, then it is possible that important information may be
missed. In the examples in Figure 3, the grain orientations normal to this plane appear to be
randomly distributed. However, if the orientations are viewed from directions within the
plane of the map/sample, then a different picture emerges. Figure 4 shows IPF colour scale
maps for the three orthogonal directions on the sample (now oriented so that the AM growth
direction is vertically upward in the plane of the maps). The predominance of green hues in
Figure 4c show there is a preferred <101> orientation in the direction of growth, but with no
preferential rotation about this axis. Additionally Figure 4c makes a change in preferred
orientation more visible at the outer edges of the sample above the level at which the sample
diameter increases to a preferred orientation. An increase in red colour in these regions
shows a tendency towards the red/cubic <100> aligned with the growth direction; a change in
this region was just about visible in the IPF(z) map of Figure 4a but was less prominent and
more difficult to interpret.

Binary colour scales such as those shown in the preceding Figure 16 may therefore be easier to
interpret, particularly when primarily the extreme values such as the largest or most elongated
grains.

4.2 Use of grey scale maps

Possibly the best approach for such circumstances is to use a grey scale with a linear gradient
between black and white, and to use the scale limits to highlight the required information.
Figure 18 a) and b) show examples of this for the grain size and aspect ratio maps.





                                      Page 28 of 35  a)                    b)                        c)                    d)





  Figure 18. Grey scale maps showing a) Aspect ratios (0.04-0.5) and b) Aspect ratios 0.04-0.25: c) Circle
            equivalent diameter grain size (30-321 µm) and d) as c) but size range 100-321 µm.


The grey scale shown in Figure 18 is the default scale produced by a manufacturer’s EBSD
software and it can be verified readily that it has a linear transition from black (0) to white
(255) on an 8 bit greyscale. However, when the actual greyscale values plotted on an example
map are compared with the corresponding grain size (circle equivalent diameter), it is found
that in plotting the map, a gamma correction has been applied which accentuates the
variation between larger grains in the map and reduces it for the smaller grains (Figure 19).


          a)                                   b)





   Figure 19. a) Enlargement of a region of the sample shown in Figure 18, with the reported grey scale
shown and b) a graph of the grey scale showing linear decrease of reported grey scale (blue line) compared
          with actual grey scale-grain size correspondences measured for a range of grain sizes.


The use of grey scale maps also allows for the rapid assessment of variability with position.
Using an image analysis program such as ImageJ, the brightness profile of a broad line drawn
across the sample at any given position will give a plot of the average grain size. This avoids
the need to divide the map data into subsets and overcomes the difficulties of the subsequent
subsets only including partial data for the grains intersected by the subset borders. Although
the grey scales do not give the grain size immediately (and as plotted will give an inverted view



                                      Page 29 of 35of the size if white = 255), a simple linear conversion can produce the graphs shown below in
Figure 20 c) and d). However, the linear correction gives a mean value lower than the true
value because of the (undefined) gamma correction noted in Figure 19. With further
correction for this gamma correction, the values should correspond to an area weighted mean
value. Even without correction, these graphs clearly quantify trends in average values with
lateral and vertical positions, and the degree of local uniformity which otherwise would be
difficult to describe.


     a)                                            b)





       c)                                       d)





 Figure 20. a) Grain size (30 – 321 µm) and b) aspect ratio (0.04 – 0.25) grey scale maps showing 100 pixel
  wide (|0.8 mm) bands on maps reduced to 1024 pixels height for measurement of features. c) 25 point
     moving average graphs of grey scale converted to circle equivalent diameter assuming a linear
                              transformation, d) as c) but for aspect ratio.





                                      Page 30 of 354.3 Summary

    •   Colour and grey scale maps can be used to show the uniformity or otherwise of
          microstructural parameters over large areas
    •    Scales which have transitions between colours or grey levels can appear similar but
        need to be carefully defined so the similarity can be established before comparisons
         are made.
    •   Even when a map’s colour (grey) scale is shown, the actual correspondence between
         the map parameter and the scale may be distorted
    •   Image analysis of grey scale maps can be used as a quick and simple way to plot
          variation with position in large scale maps

James A. D. Ball, Anna Kareer, Oxana V. Magdysyuk, Stefan Michalik, Thomas Connolley, and David M. Collins. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2302.10711, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2302.10711. This article has 6 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The HR-EBSD method measures residual elastic strain by extracting a reference EBSP (Electron BackScatter Pattern) within a grain and measuring image shifts via cross-correlation between the reference pattern and test patterns. A deformation gradient tensor is derived from the diffraction pattern shifts, allowing separation of strain and rotation components using a finite decomposition framework. The resulting strain tensor is multiplied by the stiffness tensor for ferritic steel to obtain the stress tensor. The method has a strain sensitivity of at least 1 × 10⁻⁴. However, the excerpt does not contain information addressing crack tip stress fields or dislocation characterization. The excerpt discusses the use of EBSD data for generating synthetic microstructure datasets and reduced-order models. Grain morphology and lattice orientation (crystallographic texture) are key EBSD-derived characteristics represented in synthetic structures using Dream3D software. The number of grains in synthetic structures typically varies from tens to thousands depending on computational resources. Since full EBSD datasets may contain hundreds to thousands of grains, representative volume elements (RVEs) are created with reduced grain numbers to manage computational costs while maintaining accurate representation of microstructural characteristics. Generating accurate reduced-order Euler angle datasets from EBSD measurements is important not only for crystal plasticity simulations but also for surrogate modeling and reduced-order modeling approaches that streamline complex physical models while maintaining accuracy.

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| EBSD Measurement | Key Sensitivity Parameters | Documented Bias/Variability | Relevant Standards | Robustness Rating |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grain size and grain size distribution | Step size/pixel size; grain-definition misorientation threshold; minimum grain size cutoff; treatment of non-indexed points; cleanup; number- vs area-weighting; binning method | In a recrystallized equiaxed alloy, changing GB threshold from 5° to 15° changed mean ECD by **<7%**; in AM datasets, minimum-pixel cutoff and pixel size changed reported mean grain size by about **20%** for number-average metrics; area-weighted metrics were less step-size dependent and better discriminated broad distributions; histogram binning materially changes visual conclusions (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026) | **ISO 13067:2020** for average grain size; **ASTM E2627** commonly referenced for EBSD grain-size practice; NPL guide stresses reporting exact definition/software (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000052) | **Moderate–Robust** |
| Grain morphology / aspect ratio | Step size; segmentation method; ellipse-fitting algorithm; Feret definition; software package; scale range and map visualization choices | Same AM sample analyzed by two vendor packages gave ~**20%** difference in major-axis value after accounting for radius/diameter convention, and inverse aspect-ratio conventions (e.g., 3.3 vs 0.27) can invert interpretation; circularity is highly step-size sensitive because perimeter is discretization-sensitive (pqac-00000027) | No single universal morphology standard inside EBSD software; report definitions/software explicitly; NPL warns defaults differ across vendors (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000052) | **Fragile** |
| Crystallographic texture (ODF, pole figures, texture index) | Sample-axis registration; microscope/EBSD axis calibration; section plane selection; map area representativeness; color scale/IPF choice; reduction/sampling method | Losing AM X-Y-Z orientation can make texture-property interpretation impossible; viewing only one IPF direction can hide strong preferred orientation visible on orthogonal maps; color scales and plotting choices can materially alter apparent heterogeneity even for identical data (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052) | No single texture-only standard cited here; best practice is explicit axis definition and complete reporting of section/sample orientation (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052) | **Moderate** |
| Misorientation distribution and GBCD (including network/connectivity) | Misorientation tolerance; CSL tolerance criterion; cleanup near boundaries; minimum segment length; 2D vs 3D acquisition; stereological assumptions; texture dependence for planar methods | Boundary classification shifts with tolerance choices; coherent vs slightly incoherent Σ3 boundaries can change corrosion/passivation interpretation, with a critical transition reported around **0.4–0.5°** deviation from ideal Σ3 geometry; 2D analyses can miss true connectivity and plane information needed for network conclusions (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039) | No universal consensus standard for 5-parameter GBCD in routine EBSD; reporting of Brandon/CSL criteria and 2D/3D method is essential (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039) | **Moderate–Fragile** |
| KAM, GOS, and GND density | Step size; neighbor order/kernel size; denoising/cleanup; angular resolution/noise floor; boundary exclusion rules; differentiation scheme for GND | KAM is explicitly step-size dependent; local misorientation metrics can be inflated or suppressed by cleanup and kernel definition; GND maps inherit orientation-noise amplification because they require spatial gradients of orientation; interpretation near crack tips and boundaries is especially sensitive to spatial resolution (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000055) | No broadly adopted standard for KAM/GOS/GND reporting; must state step size, kernel, excluded boundaries, and smoothing/cleanup choices (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000025) | **Fragile** |
| Residual elastic strain and stress via HR-EBSD / cross-correlation | Pattern quality; reference pattern choice; detector calibration; surface preparation/edge rounding; strain-free reference assumption; spatial step size; stiffness tensor choice | HR-EBSD offers strain sensitivity of at least **1×10^-4**, but results depend strongly on reference selection and pattern quality; preparation artifacts such as edge rounding can bias crack-tip fields, so papers explicitly note when such errors were avoided (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000055) | No mature universal standard cited here for HR-EBSD stress mapping; full reporting of cross-correlation setup and elastic constants is necessary (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054) | **Fragile** |
| Phase fraction and phase identification | Pattern indexing method; phase library completeness; pseudosymmetry; step size relative to phase size; confidence-index filtering; overlap with second phases | Small or thin second phases are easily missed when step size exceeds feature size; confidence-index filtering can preferentially delete minority-phase pixels; nanoscale phases are often below conventional EBSD spatial resolution and require transmission/HR approaches or correlative methods (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050) | No specific standard cited here beyond normal EBSD reporting practice; phase list/indexing settings must be disclosed | **Moderate–Fragile** |
| Twin and variant analysis | Angular tolerance to ideal twin/variant relation; step size relative to twin thickness/lath width; cleanup that merges thin twins; parent OR assumption | Twin-related conclusions are sensitive to whether boundaries remain coherent versus slightly deviated; thin twins/variants can be lost by coarse step size or cleanup; variant pairing and packet assignment depend on the assumed orientation relationship and reconstruction workflow (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030) | No single standard cited; explicit twin criterion, OR, and pixel/cleanup rules required (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030) | **Fragile** |
| Parent-phase reconstruction (prior-austenite / prior-beta) | Choice/refinement of orientation relationship; graph-clustering parameters; tolerance for child-parent assignment; retained parent fraction; twin handling | Reconstructed parent grains and packet/variant identities can change if OR is not iteratively refined; annealing twins and partial transformations complicate segmentation; therefore property conclusions based on prior-grain size are workflow-sensitive (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000045) | No universal standard; MTEX/related workflows improve transparency but require full disclosure of OR refinement and clustering settings (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000031) | **Fragile** |
| 3D EBSD / serial sectioning derived statistics | Slice thickness; registration accuracy; missing/poor slices; voxel anisotropy; cleanup between slices; segmentation misorientation tolerance | 3D reconstruction quality is highly sensitive to registration and segmentation tolerance; cloud-based reprocessing of TriBeam data showed grain segmentation tolerance can bias reconstructed grain sizes; 3D EBSD is uniquely valuable because 2D can misstate connectivity and true grain shape, but acquisition burden and slice loss remain major limitations (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000056) | No universal 3D EBSD standard cited here; best practice is complete reporting of voxel size, registration, and segmentation parameters (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000056) | **Fragile** |


*Table: This table summarizes which EBSD-derived measurements are most sensitive to acquisition and post-processing choices, and where the literature documents materially different outcomes. {"answer": "# Quantitative Microstructural Outcomes from EBSD: A Prioritized Evidence-Based Survey

## 1. Which EBSD-Derived Quantities Matter Most Now

The following ranking table synthesizes the current importance, research activity, property linkage strength, reproducibility, and computational demand for each major EBSD-derived measurement category.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Crystallographic texture** (ODF, pole figures, texture index) stands at the top of this ranking. It is the single most widely demanded EBSD output for both research and industry because it directly governs macroscopic elastic and plastic anisotropy through the fundamental relationship between crystal orientation and slip system activation described by Schmid's law (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018). Texture also serves as the primary input for crystal plasticity modeling pipelines (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000056). Measuring distances between crystallographic textures is recognized as essential for materials design and optimal process control in the metal industry (pqac-00000019).

**Grain size and grain size distribution** is the second most important quantity, underpinning the Hall-Petch relationship and serving as a mandatory input for generating initial microstructures in full-field modeling and for material parameter identification associated with microstructure evolution (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000003). Volume-weighted average grain size has been shown to produce a better-fitting Hall-Petch relationship compared to simple number-averaged grain size (pqac-00000022).

**Misorientation distribution and GBCD** rank third. The fraction, connectivity, and character of grain boundaries—particularly the distinction between special (CSL) and random high-angle boundaries—has direct, quantitative implications for intergranular corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, and corrosion fatigue (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014).

**KAM, GOS, and GND density** are among the most frequently reported EBSD metrics in the literature, used to characterize local plastic strain, deformation heterogeneity, and recrystallization state (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000022). However, their property linkage is weaker than often assumed, and they suffer from significant step-size dependence, placing them lower in the overall importance ranking for decision-making purposes.

**HR-EBSD** for residual elastic strain/stress measurement offers strain sensitivity of at least 1 × 10⁻⁴ (pqac-00000053) and has demonstrated capability for mapping crack-tip stress fields and dislocation structures (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055), but remains a specialist technique with high acquisition burden and limited standardization.

**3D EBSD** serial sectioning provides uniquely valuable true connectivity and five-parameter grain boundary plane data. The five-parameter grain boundary character distribution (GBCD) relates grain boundary area to energy and reveals that frequently observed boundary planes tend to have the lowest energy (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043). However, 3D EBSD datasets remain rare and resource-intensive.

## 2. Structure–Property Linkage

### Strongest demonstrated property payoff

**Texture → anisotropy.** Crystallographic texture is the primary source of both elastic and plastic anisotropy. In LPBF 316L stainless steel, moderate texture produces ~15% yield-strength variation between build directions (X: 581 MPa vs Z: 506–514 MPa), while extreme Goss texture (21 m.u.d.) creates ~30% strength differences between ⟨111⟩ and ⟨100⟩ directions (pqac-00000017). Crystal plasticity models calibrated with EBSD texture data can predict stress–strain response within 5% error. Elongation varies from 36.2% to 96.3% depending on crystal orientation relative to load, further demonstrating that texture dominates over grain morphology and porosity as the primary source of mechanical anisotropy in AM metals (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

**Grain size → yield strength (Hall-Petch).** The fundamental grain-size–strength relationship is well established. EBSD enables not only mean grain size measurement but full grain size distribution characterization, with the volume-weighted average providing the most physically meaningful input for Hall-Petch predictions (pqac-00000022). In crystal plasticity frameworks, EBSD-measured grain sizes are used to calculate slip-system-level micro-Hall-Petch parameters via the Saltykov method for 2D-to-3D conversion (pqac-00000003).

**GBCD → corrosion and SCC.** Grain boundary engineering to increase the fraction of special boundaries (particularly Σ3) to ~74% has demonstrated strong improvements in SCC resistance. In 304 stainless steel, GBE treatment produced fewer secondary cracks and more tortuous intergranular crack paths (pqac-00000014). In 316L, optimal GBE conditions achieved the longest corrosion fatigue life of 3,187 cycles, with Σ3 boundaries showing ~3.5× less corrosion depth than random high-angle boundaries (210 nm vs 60 nm) (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013). However, special boundaries resist intergranular corrosion but do not effectively block transgranular fatigue crack propagation (pqac-00000011). On copper, EBSD revealed that the passivation efficiency of Σ3 boundaries transitions sharply at deviation angles of 0.4–0.5° from ideal coherent geometry (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).

**Orientation and Schmid factor → fatigue crack initiation.** In rolled Ti-6Al-4V, EBSD analysis of 596 crack segments showed that fatigue cracks initiate preferentially on prismatic slip systems in grains with very high Schmid factors (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034). At grain boundaries, crack deflection is governed by the interplay between the geometric compatibility factor and the Schmid factor in neighboring grains (pqac-00000032). This demonstrates a strong, quantitative link between EBSD-measured local orientation data and fatigue crack path prediction.

**Prior-austenite grain size → toughness and martensite hierarchy.** In LPBF 17-4 PH steel, smaller prior austenite grains (~10.2 µm) led to improved grain boundary connectivity and higher length fractions of desirable intervariant boundaries (60°/[11̄1] and 10.5°/[011]), with implications for toughness, strength, intergranular corrosion, and cracking behavior (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047). Martensitic transformation increases mechanical strength through Hall-Petch hardening via hierarchical subdivision of parent grains into child domains (pqac-00000029).

### Most often reported but weakly linked

**KAM/GOS/GND density** are extremely widely reported as qualitative indicators of deformation state, but their quantitative structure–property predictions remain weak because the metrics are inherently step-size dependent and lack standardized reporting conventions, making cross-study comparison unreliable (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000022).

**Grain morphology (aspect ratio)** is frequently reported in AM studies, but its isolated contribution to mechanical properties is typically secondary to texture effects. In multiple LPBF alloy reviews, texture was identified as a greater contributor to strength anisotropy than grain shape alone (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020).

## 3. Emerging and High-Growth Uses (2020–2026)

### CPFEM and ICME

The primary EBSD inputs for crystal plasticity simulations are crystallographic orientation data (Euler angles), grain size distributions, and grain morphology. EBSD maps are used to construct representative volume elements (RVEs), with each voxel assigned a distinct orientation from the measured texture (pqac-00000002). The PRISMS-Plasticity pipeline, for example, generates starting microstructures from input EBSD data or synthetic textures for Taylor-type crystal plasticity modeling (pqac-00000004). Accurate reduced-order Euler angle datasets that faithfully represent crystallographic texture are essential for these workflows; the TACS (texture adaptive clustering and sampling) method achieved Kolmogorov-Smirnov test scores near 0.9 for texture fidelity, compared to below 0.3 for conventional EBSD dataset reduction (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000056).

### Synthetic microstructure generation

DREAM.3D and related tools require EBSD-derived orientation distributions and grain size distributions (including 2D-to-3D conversion via the Saltykov method) as input for generating synthetic polycrystalline microstructures (pqac-00000003). Grain morphology (shape parameters) is also needed but is more difficult to standardize. The availability of high-quality EBSD texture and grain-size data is the actual bottleneck for these workflows, rather than the computational tools themselves.

### Machine learning surrogate models

ML approaches increasingly use texture representations (ODFs, pole figure images, orientation histograms) as features for microstructure–property regression. Novel distance measures based on Earth Mover's Distance have been introduced for quantifying texture similarity, which is essential for materials design and process optimization applications (pqac-00000019). Transfer learning approaches have been applied to EBSD pattern classification (pqac-00000019).

### Digital twins and AM qualification

For additive manufacturing, the dominant EBSD-derived inputs to digital twin and qualification frameworks are crystallographic texture (which controls anisotropy), grain morphology (columnar vs equiaxed), and defect/porosity metrics. Physics-based models require EBSD texture measurements to isolate and predict the contribution of each anisotropy source to specific alloys and LPBF processes (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000021).

## 4. Additive Manufacturing Specifically

### Most reported and decision-relevant EBSD outcomes for LPBF

**Crystallographic texture** is identified as the most critical EBSD measurement for AM process qualification, as it is the primary source of elastic and plastic anisotropy in virtually all LPBF metals (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). In LPBF 316L, texture measured by EBSD directly predicts yield-stress and elongation anisotropy and can be used to calibrate crystal plasticity simulations (pqac-00000017). For LPBF Ti-6Al-4V, reconstructed β-phase texture from EBSD reveals ⟨100⟩ fiber texture aligned with the build direction, with alignment disappearing after heat treatment above the α→β transformation temperature (pqac-00000028).

**Columnar vs equiaxed grain morphology** is the second most-reported outcome. Grain elongation in the solidification direction shows periodic variation from melting/remelting patterns; preferentially oriented grains grow at the expense of others, creating wide or bimodal size distributions (pqac-00000006). The NPL guide emphasizes that single mean values of grain size can be meaningless for AM materials without proper context about the distribution and calculation method used (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000025).

**Cell/subgrain structure in AlSi10Mg.** The as-built SLM AlSi10Mg microstructure consists of heterogeneous zones: fine melt-pool cells, coarse melt-pool regions, and heat-affected zones, all composed of primary α-Al cells surrounded by a continuous cellular Si network (pqac-00000049). EBSD combined with XRD tracks cell size evolution through heat treatment and severe plastic deformation, with ECAP reducing grain size from ~1.42 µm to ~0.24 µm after two passes (pqac-00000049). The corrosion resistance of AlSi10Mg improved significantly after ECAP processing, with polarization resistance increasing from ~1.1 kΩ·cm² (as-built) to ~75.5 kΩ·cm² (2 ECAP passes) (pqac-00000050).

**Melt-pool boundary structure and LAGB/HAGB fractions** are widely reported but their isolated contribution to properties is difficult to separate from texture effects. Melt pools primarily affect elongation and ductility rather than strength (pqac-00000009).

**Prior-austenite reconstruction in LPBF steels** is emerging as a high-value technique. In LPBF 17-4 PH steel, five-parameter characterization of intervariant boundaries showed that smaller prior austenite grains improve the grain boundary network by increasing desirable {110} twist boundary plane populations, which are beneficial for controlling hydrogen embrittlement and dislocation plasticity (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047).

## 5. Reproducibility and Measurement-Quality Concerns

The following table summarizes where the literature has documented that acquisition and post-processing choices materially change reported results.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### Key findings on robustness vs fragility

**Most robust:** Area-weighted grain size metrics are the most reproducible EBSD outputs; they reduce dependence on step size and map quality, and better discriminate between samples with different size distributions than number-average metrics (pqac-00000026). Crystallographic texture is moderately robust if sample axis registration is rigorously controlled (pqac-00000051).

**Most fragile:** KAM, GOS, and GND density are explicitly step-size dependent. Local misorientation values scale with step size, and GND density calculations amplify orientation noise because they require spatial gradients (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000055). HR-EBSD strain mapping depends critically on reference pattern selection and surface preparation quality (pqac-00000053). Grain morphology parameters (aspect ratio, ellipticity, circularity) are highly definition-dependent: two commercial software packages analyzing the same AM sample produced ~20% differences in fitted major-axis values and reported inverse aspect-ratio conventions (3.3 vs 0.27), potentially inverting interpretation if not carefully documented (pqac-00000027). 3D EBSD statistics are fragile due to registration, segmentation tolerance, and slice-loss sensitivity (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000044).

**Standards landscape:** ISO 13067:2020 covers average grain size from EBSD, and ASTM E2627 is commonly referenced for EBSD grain-size practice (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000052). No mature universal standards exist for KAM/GOS/GND reporting, HR-EBSD stress mapping, five-parameter GBCD, or grain morphology parameter definitions. The NPL Good Practice Guide (Mingard 2023) specifically warns that different EBSD software packages use different definitions for shape parameters and color scales, and that these choices can materially alter conclusions about sample-to-sample differences (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000052).

## 6. Ranked Shortlist for Automated EBSD Parameter Optimization

The following table presents a prioritized assessment of which EBSD measurements would create the most scientific value if reliably automated with quantified uncertainty, and which are premature targets.

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

### Summary rationale

**Tier 1 (Highest Value)** comprises crystallographic texture, grain size/distribution, and grain morphology/aspect ratio. They have the strongest demonstrated property payoff (anisotropy, Hall-Petch, columnar-vs-equiaxed classification), the highest computational demand, and—critically—their reproducibility weaknesses are addressable through standardized definitions, consistent thresholds, and area-weighted metrics (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000056).

{"answer": "# Quantitative Microstructural Outcomes from EBSD: A Prioritized Evidence-Based Survey

## 1. Which EBSD-Derived Quantities Matter Most Now

The following ranking table synthesizes the current importance, research activity, property linkage strength, reproducibility, and computational demand for each major EBSD-derived measurement category.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Crystallographic texture** (ODF, pole figures, texture index) stands at the top of this ranking. It is the single most widely demanded EBSD output for both research and industry because it directly governs macroscopic elastic and plastic anisotropy through the fundamental relationship between crystal orientation and slip system activation described by Schmid's law (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018). Texture also serves as the primary input for crystal plasticity modeling pipelines (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000056). Measuring distances between crystallographic textures is recognized as essential for materials design and optimal process control in the metal industry (pqac-00000019).

**Grain size and grain size distribution** is the second most important quantity, underpinning the Hall-Petch relationship and serving as a mandatory input for generating initial microstructures in full-field modeling and for material parameter identification associated with microstructure evolution (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000003). Volume-weighted average grain size has been shown to produce a better-fitting Hall-Petch relationship compared to simple number-averaged grain size (pqac-00000022).

**Misorientation distribution and GBCD** rank third. The fraction, connectivity, and character of grain boundaries—particularly the distinction between special (CSL) and random high-angle boundaries—has direct, quantitative implications for intergranular corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, and corrosion fatigue (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014).

**KAM, GOS, and GND density** are among the most frequently reported EBSD metrics in the literature, used to characterize local plastic strain, deformation heterogeneity, and recrystallization state (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000022). However, their property linkage is weaker than often assumed, and they suffer from significant step-size dependence, placing them lower in the overall importance ranking for decision-making purposes.

**HR-EBSD** for residual elastic strain/stress measurement offers strain sensitivity of at least 1 × 10⁻⁴ (pqac-00000053) and has demonstrated capability for mapping crack-tip stress fields and dislocation structures (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055), but remains a specialist technique with high acquisition burden and limited standardization.

**3D EBSD** serial sectioning provides uniquely valuable true connectivity and five-parameter grain boundary plane data. The five-parameter grain boundary character distribution (GBCD) relates grain boundary area to energy and reveals that frequently observed boundary planes tend to have the lowest energy (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043). However, 3D EBSD datasets remain rare and resource-intensive.

## 2. Structure–Property Linkage

### Strongest demonstrated property payoff

**Texture → anisotropy.** Crystallographic texture is the primary source of both elastic and plastic anisotropy. In LPBF 316L stainless steel, moderate texture produces ~15% yield-strength variation between build directions (X: 581 MPa vs Z: 506–514 MPa), while extreme Goss texture (21 m.u.d.) creates ~30% strength differences between ⟨111⟩ and ⟨100⟩ directions (pqac-00000017). Crystal plasticity models calibrated with EBSD texture data can predict stress–strain response within 5% error. Elongation varies from 36.2% to 96.3% depending on crystal orientation relative to load, further demonstrating that texture dominates over grain morphology and porosity as the primary source of mechanical anisotropy in AM metals (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

**Grain size → yield strength (Hall-Petch).** The fundamental grain-size–strength relationship is well established. EBSD enables not only mean grain size measurement but full grain size distribution characterization, with the volume-weighted average providing the most physically meaningful input for Hall-Petch predictions (pqac-00000022). In crystal plasticity frameworks, EBSD-measured grain sizes are used to calculate slip-system-level micro-Hall-Petch parameters via the Saltykov method for 2D-to-3D conversion (pqac-00000003).

**GBCD → corrosion and SCC.** Grain boundary engineering to increase the fraction of special boundaries (particularly Σ3) to ~74% has demonstrated strong improvements in SCC resistance. In 304 stainless steel, GBE treatment produced fewer secondary cracks and more tortuous intergranular crack paths (pqac-00000014). In 316L, optimal GBE conditions achieved the longest corrosion fatigue life of 3,187 cycles, with Σ3 boundaries showing ~3.5× less corrosion depth than random high-angle boundaries (210 nm vs 60 nm) (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013). However, special boundaries resist intergranular corrosion but do not effectively block transgranular fatigue crack propagation (pqac-00000011). On copper, EBSD revealed that the passivation efficiency of Σ3 boundaries transitions sharply at deviation angles of 0.4–0.5° from ideal coherent geometry (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).

**Orientation and Schmid factor → fatigue crack initiation.** In rolled Ti-6Al-4V, EBSD analysis of 596 crack segments showed that fatigue cracks initiate preferentially on prismatic slip systems in grains with very high Schmid factors (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034). At grain boundaries, crack deflection is governed by the interplay between the geometric compatibility factor and the Schmid factor in neighboring grains (pqac-00000032). This demonstrates a strong, quantitative link between EBSD-measured local orientation data and fatigue crack path prediction.

**Prior-austenite grain size → toughness and martensite hierarchy.** In LPBF 17-4 PH steel, smaller prior austenite grains (~10.2 µm) led to improved grain boundary connectivity and higher length fractions of desirable intervariant boundaries (60°/[11̄1] and 10.5°/[011]), with implications for toughness, strength, intergranular corrosion, and cracking behavior (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047). Martensitic transformation increases mechanical strength through Hall-Petch hardening via hierarchical subdivision of parent grains into child domains (pqac-00000029).

### Most often reported but weakly linked

**KAM/GOS/GND density** are extremely widely reported as qualitative indicators of deformation state, but their quantitative structure–property predictions remain weak because the metrics are inherently step-size dependent and lack standardized reporting conventions, making cross-study comparison unreliable (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000022).

**Grain morphology (aspect ratio)** is frequently reported in AM studies, but its isolated contribution to mechanical properties is typically secondary to texture effects. In multiple LPBF alloy reviews, texture was identified as a greater contributor to strength anisotropy than grain shape alone (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020).

## 3. Emerging and High-Growth Uses (2020–2026)

### CPFEM and ICME

The primary EBSD inputs for crystal plasticity simulations are crystallographic orientation data (Euler angles), grain size distributions, and grain morphology. EBSD maps are used to construct representative volume elements (RVEs), with each voxel assigned a distinct orientation from the measured texture (pqac-00000002). The PRISMS-Plasticity pipeline, for example, generates starting microstructures from input EBSD data or synthetic textures for Taylor-type crystal plasticity modeling (pqac-00000004). Accurate reduced-order Euler angle datasets that faithfully represent crystallographic texture are essential for these workflows; the TACS (texture adaptive clustering and sampling) method achieved Kolmogorov-Smirnov test scores near 0.9 for texture fidelity, compared to below 0.3 for conventional EBSD dataset reduction (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000056).

### Synthetic microstructure generation

DREAM.3D and related tools require EBSD-derived orientation distributions and grain size distributions (including 2D-to-3D conversion via the Saltykov method) as input for generating synthetic polycrystalline microstructures (pqac-00000003). Grain morphology (shape parameters) is also needed but is more difficult to standardize. The availability of high-quality EBSD texture and grain-size data is the actual bottleneck for these workflows, rather than the computational tools themselves.

### Machine learning surrogate models

ML approaches increasingly use texture representations (ODFs, pole figure images, orientation histograms) as features for microstructure–property regression. Novel distance measures based on Earth Mover's Distance have been introduced for quantifying texture similarity, which is essential for materials design and process optimization applications (pqac-00000019). Transfer learning approaches have been applied to EBSD pattern classification (pqac-00000019).

### Digital twins and AM qualification

For additive manufacturing, the dominant EBSD-derived inputs to digital twin and qualification frameworks are crystallographic texture (which controls anisotropy), grain morphology (columnar vs equiaxed), and defect/porosity metrics. Physics-based models require EBSD texture measurements to isolate and predict the contribution of each anisotropy source to specific alloys and LPBF processes (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000021).

## 4. Additive Manufacturing Specifically

### Most reported and decision-relevant EBSD outcomes for LPBF

**Crystallographic texture** is identified as the most critical EBSD measurement for AM process qualification, as it is the primary source of elastic and plastic anisotropy in virtually all LPBF metals (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). In LPBF 316L, texture measured by EBSD directly predicts yield-stress and elongation anisotropy and can be used to calibrate crystal plasticity simulations (pqac-00000017). For LPBF Ti-6Al-4V, reconstructed β-phase texture from EBSD reveals ⟨100⟩ fiber texture aligned with the build direction, with alignment disappearing after heat treatment above the α→β transformation temperature (pqac-00000028).

**Columnar vs equiaxed grain morphology** is the second most-reported outcome. Grain elongation in the solidification direction shows periodic variation from melting/remelting patterns; preferentially oriented grains grow at the expense of others, creating wide or bimodal size distributions (pqac-00000006). The NPL guide emphasizes that single mean values of grain size can be meaningless for AM materials without proper context about the distribution and calculation method used (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000025).

**Cell/subgrain structure in AlSi10Mg.** The as-built SLM AlSi10Mg microstructure consists of heterogeneous zones: fine melt-pool cells, coarse melt-pool regions, and heat-affected zones, all composed of primary α-Al cells surrounded by a continuous cellular Si network (pqac-00000049). EBSD combined with XRD tracks cell size evolution through heat treatment and severe plastic deformation, with ECAP reducing grain size from ~1.42 µm to ~0.24 µm after two passes (pqac-00000049). The corrosion resistance of AlSi10Mg improved significantly after ECAP processing, with polarization resistance increasing from ~1.1 kΩ·cm² (as-built) to ~75.5 kΩ·cm² (2 ECAP passes) (pqac-00000050).

**Melt-pool boundary structure and LAGB/HAGB fractions** are widely reported but their isolated contribution to properties is difficult to separate from texture effects. Melt pools primarily affect elongation and ductility rather than strength (pqac-00000009).

**Prior-austenite reconstruction in LPBF steels** is emerging as a high-value technique. In LPBF 17-4 PH steel, five-parameter characterization of intervariant boundaries showed that smaller prior austenite grains improve the grain boundary network by increasing desirable {110} twist boundary plane populations, which are beneficial for controlling hydrogen embrittlement and dislocation plasticity (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047).

## 5. Reproducibility and Measurement-Quality Concerns

The following table summarizes where the literature has documented that acquisition and post-processing choices materially change reported results.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### Key findings on robustness vs fragility

**Most robust:** Area-weighted grain size metrics are the most reproducible EBSD outputs; they reduce dependence on step size and map quality, and better discriminate between samples with different size distributions than number-average metrics (pqac-00000026). Crystallographic texture is moderately robust if sample axis registration is rigorously controlled (pqac-00000051).

**Most fragile:** KAM, GOS, and GND density are explicitly step-size dependent. Local misorientation values scale with step size, and GND density calculations amplify orientation noise because they require spatial gradients (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000055). HR-EBSD strain mapping depends critically on reference pattern selection and surface preparation quality (pqac-00000053). Grain morphology parameters (aspect ratio, ellipticity, circularity) are highly definition-dependent: two commercial software packages analyzing the same AM sample produced ~20% differences in fitted major-axis values and reported inverse aspect-ratio conventions (3.3 vs 0.27), potentially inverting interpretation if not carefully documented (pqac-00000027). 3D EBSD statistics are fragile due to registration, segmentation tolerance, and slice-loss sensitivity (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000044).

**Standards landscape:** ISO 13067:2020 covers average grain size from EBSD, and ASTM E2627 is commonly referenced for EBSD grain-size practice (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000052). No mature universal standards exist for KAM/GOS/GND reporting, HR-EBSD stress mapping, five-parameter GBCD, or grain morphology parameter definitions. The NPL Good Practice Guide (Mingard 2023) specifically warns that different EBSD software packages use different definitions for shape parameters and color scales, and that these choices can materially alter conclusions about sample-to-sample differences (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000052).

The following table presents a prioritized assessment of which EBSD measurements would create the most scientific value if reliably automated with quantified uncertainty, and which are premature targets.

**Tier 3 (Moderate Value)** covers KAM/GOS/GND density and twin/variant analysis. Although extremely popular in publications, KAM and GND density are poor early-stage automation targets because their inherent step-size dependence means that optimized acquisition parameters will change the absolute values of these metrics, creating a reproducibility paradox unless uncertainty is propagated explicitly (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000022).

**Tier 4 (Premature/Low Value for general-purpose automation)** includes HR-EBSD strain mapping and 3D EBSD statistics. Both are scientifically powerful but too fragile, labor-intensive, and under-standardized for broad automated optimization at present (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000044). They are best pursued as later-stage extensions after robust 2D workflows are established.

In conclusion, an automated EBSD parameter-optimization tool would create the most immediate scientific and industrial value by targeting crystallographic texture, grain size distribution (with area-weighted metrics and explicit threshold reporting per ISO 13067), and standardized grain morphology descriptors as its primary outputs. Misorientation/GBCD and phase identification are strong secondary targets. **Crystallographic texture** (ODF, pole figures, texture index) stands at the top of this ranking. It is the single most widely demanded EBSD output for both research and industry because it directly governs macroscopic elastic and plastic anisotropy through the fundamental relationship between crystal orientation and slip system activation described by Schmid's law (weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 10-12, weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 8-10). Texture also serves as the primary input for crystal plasticity modeling pipelines (wanni2024machinelearningenhanced pages 1-2). Measuring distances between crystallographic textures is recognized as essential for materials design and optimal process control in the metal industry (iraki2024accuratedistancesmeasures pages 1-3).

**Grain size and grain size distribution** is the second most important quantity, underpinning the Hall-Petch relationship and serving as a mandatory input for generating initial microstructures in full-field modeling and for material parameter identification associated with microstructure evolution (flipon2021grainsizecharacterization pages 1-2, lakshmanan2022crystalplasticityconstitutive pages 138-143). Volume-weighted average grain size has been shown to produce a better-fitting Hall-Petch relationship compared to simple number-averaged grain size (flipon2021grainsizecharacterization pages 1-2).

**Misorientation distribution and GBCD** rank third. The fraction, connectivity, and character of grain boundaries—particularly the distinction between special (CSL) and random high-angle boundaries—has direct, quantitative implications for intergranular corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, and corrosion fatigue (zhang2022effectsofgrain pages 4-6, barr2018trackingtheevolution pages 2-3, zhang2022effectsofgrain pages 1-2, liu2019grainboundaryengineering pages 6-8).

**KAM, GOS, and GND density** are among the most frequently reported EBSD metrics in the literature, used to characterize local plastic strain, deformation heterogeneity, and recrystallization state (roy2026themechanisticaspects pages 34-43, flipon2021grainsizecharacterization pages 1-2). However, their property linkage is weaker than often assumed, and they suffer from significant step-size dependence, placing them lower in the overall importance ranking for decision-making purposes.

**HR-EBSD** for residual elastic strain/stress measurement offers strain sensitivity of at least 1 × 10⁻⁴ (ball2023pergrainandneighbourhood pages 3-4) and has demonstrated capability for mapping crack-tip stress fields and dislocation structures (roy2026themechanisticaspects pages 43-46, roy2026themechanisticaspects pages 11-15), but remains a specialist technique with high acquisition burden and limited standardization.

**3D EBSD** serial sectioning provides uniquely valuable true connectivity and five-parameter grain boundary plane data. The five-parameter grain boundary character distribution (GBCD) relates grain boundary area to energy and reveals that frequently observed boundary planes tend to have the lowest energy (marquardt2018thestructureand pages 9-13, dillon2022grainboundaryenergies pages 2-2, marquardt2018thestructureand pages 6-9, dillon2022grainboundaryenergies pages 3-3). However, 3D EBSD datasets remain rare and resource-intensive.

## 2. Structure–Property Linkage

### Strongest demonstrated property payoff

**Texture → anisotropy.** Crystallographic texture is the primary source of both elastic and plastic anisotropy. In LPBF 316L stainless steel, moderate texture produces ~15% yield-strength variation between build directions (X: 581 MPa vs Z: 506–514 MPa), while extreme Goss texture (21 m.u.d.) creates ~30% strength differences between ⟨111⟩ and ⟨100⟩ directions (weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 10-12). Crystal plasticity models calibrated with EBSD texture data can predict stress–strain response within 5% error. Elongation varies from 36.2% to 96.3% depending on crystal orientation relative to load, further demonstrating that texture dominates over grain morphology and porosity as the primary source of mechanical anisotropy in AM metals (weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 10-12, weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 12-15, weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 25-27).

**Grain size → yield strength (Hall-Petch).** The fundamental grain-size–strength relationship is well established. EBSD enables not only mean grain size measurement but full grain size distribution characterization, with the volume-weighted average providing the most physically meaningful input for Hall-Petch predictions (flipon2021grainsizecharacterization pages 1-2). In crystal plasticity frameworks, EBSD-measured grain sizes are used to calculate slip-system-level micro-Hall-Petch parameters via the Saltykov method for 2D-to-3D conversion (lakshmanan2022crystalplasticityconstitutive pages 138-143).

**GBCD → corrosion and SCC.** Grain boundary engineering to increase the fraction of special boundaries (particularly Σ3) to ~74% has demonstrated strong improvements in SCC resistance. In 304 stainless steel, GBE treatment produced fewer secondary cracks and more tortuous intergranular crack paths (liu2019grainboundaryengineering pages 6-8). In 316L, optimal GBE conditions achieved the longest corrosion fatigue life of 3,187 cycles, with Σ3 boundaries showing ~3.5× less corrosion depth than random high-angle boundaries (210 nm vs 60 nm) (zhang2022effectsofgrain pages 4-6, zhang2022effectsofgrain pages 1-2). However, special boundaries resist intergranular corrosion but do not effectively block transgranular fatigue crack propagation (zhang2022effectsofgrain pages 4-6). On copper, EBSD revealed that the passivation efficiency of Σ3 boundaries transitions sharply at deviation angles of 0.4–0.5° from ideal coherent geometry (bettayeb2019combinedinsitu pages 9-13, bettayeb2019combinedinsitu pages 13-18).

**Orientation and Schmid factor → fatigue crack initiation.** In rolled Ti-6Al-4V, EBSD analysis of 596 crack segments showed that fatigue cracks initiate preferentially on prismatic slip systems in grains with very high Schmid factors (briffod2019effectofcrystallographic pages 24-28, briffod2019effectofcrystallographic pages 7-11, briffod2019effectofcrystallographic pages 1-4). At grain boundaries, crack deflection is governed by the interplay between the geometric compatibility factor and the Schmid factor in neighboring grains (briffod2019effectofcrystallographic pages 24-28). This demonstrates a strong, quantitative link between EBSD-measured local orientation data and fatigue crack path prediction.

**Prior-austenite grain size → toughness and martensite hierarchy.** In LPBF 17-4 PH steel, smaller prior austenite grains (~10.2 µm) led to improved grain boundary connectivity and higher length fractions of desirable intervariant boundaries (60°/[11̄1] and 10.5°/[011]), with implications for toughness, strength, intergranular corrosion, and cracking behavior (haines2025onthemartensitic pages 1-3, haines2025onthemartensitic pages 13-15). Martensitic transformation increases mechanical strength through Hall-Petch hardening via hierarchical subdivision of parent grains into child domains (niessen2022parentgrainreconstruction pages 1-4).

### Most often reported but weakly linked

**KAM/GOS/GND density** are extremely widely reported as qualitative indicators of deformation state, but their quantitative structure–property predictions remain weak because the metrics are inherently step-size dependent and lack standardized reporting conventions, making cross-study comparison unreliable (roy2026themechanisticaspects pages 34-43, flipon2021grainsizecharacterization pages 1-2).

**Grain morphology (aspect ratio)** is frequently reported in AM studies, but its isolated contribution to mechanical properties is typically secondary to texture effects. In multiple LPBF alloy reviews, texture was identified as a greater contributor to strength anisotropy than grain shape alone (weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 10-12, weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 12-15).

## 3. Emerging and High-Growth Uses (2020–2026)

### CPFEM and ICME

The primary EBSD inputs for crystal plasticity simulations are crystallographic orientation data (Euler angles), grain size distributions, and grain morphology. EBSD maps are used to construct representative volume elements (RVEs), with each voxel assigned a distinct orientation from the measured texture (lakshmanan2022crystalplasticityconstitutive pages 74-81). The PRISMS-Plasticity pipeline, for example, generates starting microstructures from input EBSD data or synthetic textures for Taylor-type crystal plasticity modeling (wanni2024machinelearningenhanced pages 1-2). Accurate reduced-order Euler angle datasets that faithfully represent crystallographic texture are essential for these workflows; the TACS (texture adaptive clustering and sampling) method achieved Kolmogorov-Smirnov test scores near 0.9 for texture fidelity, compared to below 0.3 for conventional EBSD dataset reduction (wanni2024machinelearningenhanced pages 1-2).

### Synthetic microstructure generation

DREAM.3D and related tools require EBSD-derived orientation distributions and grain size distributions (including 2D-to-3D conversion via the Saltykov method) as input for generating synthetic polycrystalline microstructures (lakshmanan2022crystalplasticityconstitutive pages 138-143). Grain morphology (shape parameters) is also needed but is more difficult to standardize. The availability of high-quality EBSD texture and grain-size data is the actual bottleneck for these workflows, rather than the computational tools themselves.

### Machine learning surrogate models

ML approaches increasingly use texture representations (ODFs, pole figure images, orientation histograms) as features for microstructure–property regression. Novel distance measures based on Earth Mover's Distance have been introduced for quantifying texture similarity, which is essential for materials design and process optimization applications (iraki2024accuratedistancesmeasures pages 1-3). Transfer learning approaches have been applied to EBSD pattern classification (iraki2024accuratedistancesmeasures pages 1-3).

### Digital twins and AM qualification

For additive manufacturing, the dominant EBSD-derived inputs to digital twin and qualification frameworks are crystallographic texture (which controls anisotropy), grain morphology (columnar vs equiaxed), and defect/porosity metrics. Physics-based models require EBSD texture measurements to isolate and predict the contribution of each anisotropy source to specific alloys and LPBF processes (weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 25-27).

## 4. Additive Manufacturing Specifically

### Most reported and decision-relevant EBSD outcomes for LPBF

**Crystallographic texture** is identified as the most critical EBSD measurement for AM process qualification, as it is the primary source of elastic and plastic anisotropy in virtually all LPBF metals (weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 10-12, weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 8-10, weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 12-15, weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 25-27). In LPBF 316L, texture measured by EBSD directly predicts yield-stress and elongation anisotropy and can be used to calibrate crystal plasticity simulations (weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 10-12). For LPBF Ti-6Al-4V, reconstructed β-phase texture from EBSD reveals ⟨100⟩ fiber texture aligned with the build direction, with alignment disappearing after heat treatment above the α→β transformation temperature (niessen2022parentgrainreconstruction pages 27-30).

**Columnar vs equiaxed grain morphology** is the second most-reported outcome. Grain elongation in the solidification direction shows periodic variation from melting/remelting patterns; preferentially oriented grains grow at the expense of others, creating wide or bimodal size distributions (mingard2023theuseof pages 15-20). The NPL guide emphasizes that single mean values of grain size can be meaningless for AM materials without proper context about the distribution and calculation method used (mingard2023theuseof pages 15-20, mingard2023theuseof pages 1-8).

**Cell/subgrain structure in AlSi10Mg.** The as-built SLM AlSi10Mg microstructure consists of heterogeneous zones: fine melt-pool cells, coarse melt-pool regions, and heat-affected zones, all composed of primary α-Al cells surrounded by a continuous cellular Si network (snopinski2022evolutionofmicrostructure pages 4-6). EBSD combined with XRD tracks cell size evolution through heat treatment and severe plastic deformation, with ECAP reducing grain size from ~1.42 µm to ~0.24 µm after two passes (snopinski2022evolutionofmicrostructure pages 4-6). The corrosion resistance of AlSi10Mg improved significantly after ECAP processing, with polarization resistance increasing from ~1.1 kΩ·cm² (as-built) to ~75.5 kΩ·cm² (2 ECAP passes) (snopinski2022evolutionofmicrostructure pages 9-12).

**Melt-pool boundary structure and LAGB/HAGB fractions** are widely reported but their isolated contribution to properties is difficult to separate from texture effects. Melt pools primarily affect elongation and ductility rather than strength (weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 25-27).

**Prior-austenite reconstruction in LPBF steels** is emerging as a high-value technique. In LPBF 17-4 PH steel, five-parameter characterization of intervariant boundaries showed that smaller prior austenite grains improve the grain boundary network by increasing desirable {110} twist boundary plane populations, which are beneficial for controlling hydrogen embrittlement and dislocation plasticity (haines2025onthemartensitic pages 1-3, haines2025onthemartensitic pages 13-15).

### Key findings on robustness vs fragility

**Most robust:** Area-weighted grain size metrics are the most reproducible EBSD outputs; they reduce dependence on step size and map quality, and better discriminate between samples with different size distributions than number-average metrics (mingard2023theuseof pages 24-29). Crystallographic texture is moderately robust if sample axis registration is rigorously controlled (mingard2023theuseof pages 8-15).

**Most fragile:** KAM, GOS, and GND density are explicitly step-size dependent. Local misorientation values scale with step size, and GND density calculations amplify orientation noise because they require spatial gradients (flipon2021grainsizecharacterization pages 1-2, roy2026themechanisticaspects pages 11-15). HR-EBSD strain mapping depends critically on reference pattern selection and surface preparation quality (ball2023pergrainandneighbourhood pages 3-4). Grain morphology parameters (aspect ratio, ellipticity, circularity) are highly definition-dependent: two commercial software packages analyzing the same AM sample produced ~20% differences in fitted major-axis values and reported inverse aspect-ratio conventions (3.3 vs 0.27), potentially inverting interpretation if not carefully documented (mingard2023theuseof pages 29-33). 3D EBSD statistics are fragile due to registration, segmentation tolerance, and slice-loss sensitivity (mingard2023theuseof pages 1-8, dillon2022grainboundaryenergies pages 1-2).

**Standards landscape:** ISO 13067:2020 covers average grain size from EBSD, and ASTM E2627 is commonly referenced for EBSD grain-size practice (mingard2023theuseof pages 1-8, mingard2023theuseof pages 33-41). No mature universal standards exist for KAM/GOS/GND reporting, HR-EBSD stress mapping, five-parameter GBCD, or grain morphology parameter definitions. The NPL Good Practice Guide (Mingard 2023) specifically warns that different EBSD software packages use different definitions for shape parameters and color scales, and that these choices can materially alter conclusions about sample-to-sample differences (mingard2023theuseof pages 1-8, mingard2023theuseof pages 29-33, mingard2023theuseof pages 33-41).
