| Tier 4 Premature/Low Value | Residual elastic strain/stress by HR-EBSD | Scientifically powerful with strong local-mechanics relevance, but currently too fragile, labor-intensive, and under-standardized for broad automated parameter optimization; depends on pattern quality, reference selection, and careful surface preparation, so premature as a general-purpose optimization target (ball2023pergrainandneighbourhood pages 3-4, roy2026themechanisticaspects pages 43-46, roy2026themechanisticaspects pages 11-15) |
| Tier 4 Premature/Low Value | 3D EBSD / serial sectioning derived statistics and five-parameter GBCD | Potentially transformative for true connectivity and grain-boundary-plane statistics, but acquisition burden, registration sensitivity, sparse adoption, and lack of routine standardization make it a poor early automation target except in specialized labs; best as a later-stage extension after robust 2D workflows are solved (mingard2023theuseof pages 1-8, dillon2022grainboundaryenergies pages 2-2, dillon2022grainboundaryenergies pages 1-2, wanni2024machinelearningenhanced pages 1-2) |


*Table: This table ranks EBSD-derived outputs for an automated parameter-optimization tool by expected scientific and industrial value. It prioritizes measurements that combine strong property linkage, reasonable reproducibility, and high demand in AM qualification and ICME/CPFEM workflows.*

### Summary rationale

**Tier 1 (Highest Value)** comprises crystallographic texture, grain size/distribution, and grain morphology/aspect ratio. These three outputs together form the minimal necessary input set for CPFEM, synthetic microstructure generation, and AM process qualification. They have the strongest demonstrated property payoff (anisotropy, Hall-Petch, columnar-vs-equiaxed classification), the highest computational demand, and—critically—their reproducibility weaknesses are addressable through standardized definitions, consistent thresholds, and area-weighted metrics (weaver2021understandinganisotropictensile pages 10-12, flipon2021grainsizecharacterization pages 1-2, mingard2023theuseof pages 1-8, mingard2023theuseof pages 24-29, mingard2023theuseof pages 29-33, wanni2024machinelearningenhanced pages 1-2).

**Tier 2 (High Value)** includes GBCD/misorientation distribution, phase fraction/identification, and parent-phase reconstruction. These outputs have strong property linkage in specific but industrially critical domains (stainless steels for corrosion, multiphase alloys, martensitic steels and Ti alloys), and rising demand in AM qualification. Their lower ranking reflects greater sensitivity to tolerance choices and workflow dependence (zhang2022effectsofgrain pages 4-6, liu2019grainboundaryengineering pages 6-8, niessen2022parentgrainreconstruction pages 27-30, haines2025onthemartensitic pages 1-3).

**Tier 3 (Moderate Value)** covers KAM/GOS/GND density and twin/variant analysis. Although extremely popular in publications, KAM and GND density are poor early-stage automation targets because their inherent step-size dependence means that optimized acquisition parameters will change the absolute values of these metrics, creating a reproducibility paradox unless uncertainty is propagated explicitly (roy2026themechanisticaspects pages 34-43, flipon2021grainsizecharacterization pages 1-2).

**Tier 4 (Premature/Low Value for general-purpose automation)** includes HR-EBSD strain mapping and 3D EBSD statistics. Both are scientifically powerful but too fragile, labor-intensive, and under-standardized for broad automated optimization at present (ball2023pergrainandneighbourhood pages 3-4, dillon2022grainboundaryenergies pages 1-2). They are best pursued as later-stage extensions after robust 2D workflows are established.

In conclusion, an automated EBSD parameter-optimization tool would create the most immediate scientific and industrial value by targeting crystallographic texture, grain size distribution (with area-weighted metrics and explicit threshold reporting per ISO 13067), and standardized grain morphology descriptors as its primary outputs. Misorientation/GBCD and phase identification are strong secondary targets. KAM/GOS/GND, while frequently demanded, should only be automated once their step-size dependence is explicitly addressed through uncertainty quantification. HR-EBSD and 3D EBSD are best reserved for specialized deployment.

# Quantitative Microstructural Outcomes from EBSD: A Prioritized Evidence-Based Survey

## 1. Which EBSD-Derived Quantities Matter Most Now

The following ranking table synthesizes the current importance, research activity, property linkage strength, reproducibility, and computational demand for each major EBSD-derived measurement category.

| Rank | EBSD Measurement | Property Linkage Strength | Key Properties Predicted | Reproducibility Robustness | CPFEM/ICME Demand Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Crystallographic texture (ODF, pole figures, texture intensity/index) | Strong | Elastic/plastic anisotropy, yield stress directionality, modulus, formability, ductility, AM tensile anisotropy | Moderate | Very High (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000051) |
| 2 | Grain size and grain size distribution | Strong | Yield strength, Hall-Petch behavior, hardness, recrystallization state, statistical volume element inputs | Moderate to Robust | Very High (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000006) |
| 3 | Misorientation distribution and grain boundary character distribution (GBCD, network/connectivity, 5-parameter where possible) | Strong | Intergranular corrosion, SCC, corrosion fatigue, crack path tortuosity, boundary-controlled degradation | Moderate | High (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000042) |
| 4 | Grain morphology / aspect ratio / elongation | Moderate to Strong | AM anisotropy, directional yielding, ductility, deformation partitioning, representative microstructure statistics | Fragile to Moderate | High (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000052) |
| 5 | Phase fraction and phase identification (including small second phases when resolvable) | Moderate to Strong | Strength/ductility partitioning, transformation behavior, magnetic/electrical response, fatigue and corrosion sensitivity in multiphase alloys | Moderate | High (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050) |
| 6 | KAM, GOS, and GND density | Moderate | Local plastic strain, deformation heterogeneity, fatigue initiation propensity, recovery/recrystallization state, crack-tip plasticity | Fragile | High (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000055) |
| 7 | Twin and variant analysis | Moderate | Twinning-mediated plasticity, fatigue/crack transfer pathways, corrosion arrest in twin-related domains, transformation substructure effects | Moderate to Fragile | Moderate to High (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000045) |
| 8 | Parent-phase reconstruction (prior-austenite / prior-beta) | Moderate | Toughness, strength via effective parent grain size and variant/packet hierarchy, AM martensite network design | Fragile | High in steels/Ti, Low otherwise (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047) |
| 9 | 3D EBSD / serial sectioning derived statistics | Emerging to Strong | True grain connectivity, 5-parameter boundary distributions, 3D crack/deformation path realism, validation datasets for models | Fragile | High but specialized (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000025) |
| 10 | Residual elastic strain and stress via HR-EBSD / cross-correlation | Emerging to Strong | Crack-tip fields, local stress concentrations, stored elastic strain, dislocation-stress coupling, SCC/fatigue mechanics | Fragile | Moderate to High, bottlenecked by acquisition/analysis burden (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055) |


*Table: This table ranks the main EBSD-derived quantitative outputs by current scientific and industrial importance, emphasizing property linkage, reproducibility, and demand in ICME/CPFEM workflows. It is useful as a decision aid for prioritizing which EBSD measurements merit automation and uncertainty quantification first.*

**Crystallographic texture** (ODF, pole figures, texture index) stands at the top of this ranking. It is the single most widely demanded EBSD output for both research and industry because it directly governs macroscopic elastic and plastic anisotropy through the fundamental relationship between crystal orientation and slip system activation described by Schmid's law (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018). Texture also serves as the primary input for crystal plasticity modeling pipelines (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000056). Measuring distances between crystallographic textures is recognized as essential for materials design and optimal process control in the metal industry (pqac-00000019).

**Grain size and grain size distribution** is the second most important quantity, underpinning the Hall-Petch relationship and serving as a mandatory input for generating initial microstructures in full-field modeling and for material parameter identification associated with microstructure evolution (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000003). Volume-weighted average grain size has been shown to produce a better-fitting Hall-Petch relationship compared to simple number-averaged grain size (pqac-00000022).

**Misorientation distribution and GBCD** rank third. The fraction, connectivity, and character of grain boundaries—particularly the distinction between special (CSL) and random high-angle boundaries—has direct, quantitative implications for intergranular corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, and corrosion fatigue (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014).

**KAM, GOS, and GND density** are among the most frequently reported EBSD metrics in the literature, used to characterize local plastic strain, deformation heterogeneity, and recrystallization state (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000022). However, their property linkage is weaker than often assumed, and they suffer from significant step-size dependence, placing them lower in the overall importance ranking for decision-making purposes.

**HR-EBSD** for residual elastic strain/stress measurement offers strain sensitivity of at least 1 × 10⁻⁴ (pqac-00000053) and has demonstrated capability for mapping crack-tip stress fields and dislocation structures (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055), but remains a specialist technique with high acquisition burden and limited standardization.

**3D EBSD** serial sectioning provides uniquely valuable true connectivity and five-parameter grain boundary plane data. The five-parameter grain boundary character distribution (GBCD) relates grain boundary area to energy and reveals that frequently observed boundary planes tend to have the lowest energy (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043). However, 3D EBSD datasets remain rare and resource-intensive.

## 2. Structure–Property Linkage

### Strongest demonstrated property payoff

**Texture → anisotropy.** Crystallographic texture is the primary source of both elastic and plastic anisotropy. In LPBF 316L stainless steel, moderate texture produces ~15% yield-strength variation between build directions (X: 581 MPa vs Z: 506–514 MPa), while extreme Goss texture (21 m.u.d.) creates ~30% strength differences between ⟨111⟩ and ⟨100⟩ directions (pqac-00000017). Crystal plasticity models calibrated with EBSD texture data can predict stress–strain response within 5% error. Elongation varies from 36.2% to 96.3% depending on crystal orientation relative to load, further demonstrating that texture dominates over grain morphology and porosity as the primary source of mechanical anisotropy in AM metals (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

**Grain size → yield strength (Hall-Petch).** The fundamental grain-size–strength relationship is well established. EBSD enables not only mean grain size measurement but full grain size distribution characterization, with the volume-weighted average providing the most physically meaningful input for Hall-Petch predictions (pqac-00000022). In crystal plasticity frameworks, EBSD-measured grain sizes are used to calculate slip-system-level micro-Hall-Petch parameters via the Saltykov method for 2D-to-3D conversion (pqac-00000003).

**GBCD → corrosion and SCC.** Grain boundary engineering to increase the fraction of special boundaries (particularly Σ3) to ~74% has demonstrated strong improvements in SCC resistance. In 304 stainless steel, GBE treatment produced fewer secondary cracks and more tortuous intergranular crack paths (pqac-00000014). In 316L, optimal GBE conditions achieved the longest corrosion fatigue life of 3,187 cycles, with Σ3 boundaries showing ~3.5× less corrosion depth than random high-angle boundaries (210 nm vs 60 nm) (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013). However, special boundaries resist intergranular corrosion but do not effectively block transgranular fatigue crack propagation (pqac-00000011). On copper, EBSD revealed that the passivation efficiency of Σ3 boundaries transitions sharply at deviation angles of 0.4–0.5° from ideal coherent geometry (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).

**Orientation and Schmid factor → fatigue crack initiation.** In rolled Ti-6Al-4V, EBSD analysis of 596 crack segments showed that fatigue cracks initiate preferentially on prismatic slip systems in grains with very high Schmid factors (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034). At grain boundaries, crack deflection is governed by the interplay between the geometric compatibility factor and the Schmid factor in neighboring grains (pqac-00000032). This demonstrates a strong, quantitative link between EBSD-measured local orientation data and fatigue crack path prediction.

**Prior-austenite grain size → toughness and martensite hierarchy.** In LPBF 17-4 PH steel, smaller prior austenite grains (~10.2 µm) led to improved grain boundary connectivity and higher length fractions of desirable intervariant boundaries (60°/[11̄1] and 10.5°/[011]), with implications for toughness, strength, intergranular corrosion, and cracking behavior (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047). Martensitic transformation increases mechanical strength through Hall-Petch hardening via hierarchical subdivision of parent grains into child domains (pqac-00000029).

### Most often reported but weakly linked

**KAM/GOS/GND density** are extremely widely reported as qualitative indicators of deformation state, but their quantitative structure–property predictions remain weak because the metrics are inherently step-size dependent and lack standardized reporting conventions, making cross-study comparison unreliable (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000022).

**Grain morphology (aspect ratio)** is frequently reported in AM studies, but its isolated contribution to mechanical properties is typically secondary to texture effects. In multiple LPBF alloy reviews, texture was identified as a greater contributor to strength anisotropy than grain shape alone (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020).

## 3. Emerging and High-Growth Uses (2020–2026)

### CPFEM and ICME

The primary EBSD inputs for crystal plasticity simulations are crystallographic orientation data (Euler angles), grain size distributions, and grain morphology. EBSD maps are used to construct representative volume elements (RVEs), with each voxel assigned a distinct orientation from the measured texture (pqac-00000002). The PRISMS-Plasticity pipeline, for example, generates starting microstructures from input EBSD data or synthetic textures for Taylor-type crystal plasticity modeling (pqac-00000004). Accurate reduced-order Euler angle datasets that faithfully represent crystallographic texture are essential for these workflows; the TACS (texture adaptive clustering and sampling) method achieved Kolmogorov-Smirnov test scores near 0.9 for texture fidelity, compared to below 0.3 for conventional EBSD dataset reduction (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000056).

### Synthetic microstructure generation

DREAM.3D and related tools require EBSD-derived orientation distributions and grain size distributions (including 2D-to-3D conversion via the Saltykov method) as input for generating synthetic polycrystalline microstructures (pqac-00000003). Grain morphology (shape parameters) is also needed but is more difficult to standardize. The availability of high-quality EBSD texture and grain-size data is the actual bottleneck for these workflows, rather than the computational tools themselves.

### Machine learning surrogate models

ML approaches increasingly use texture representations (ODFs, pole figure images, orientation histograms) as features for microstructure–property regression. Novel distance measures based on Earth Mover's Distance have been introduced for quantifying texture similarity, which is essential for materials design and process optimization applications (pqac-00000019). Transfer learning approaches have been applied to EBSD pattern classification (pqac-00000019).

### Digital twins and AM qualification

For additive manufacturing, the dominant EBSD-derived inputs to digital twin and qualification frameworks are crystallographic texture (which controls anisotropy), grain morphology (columnar vs equiaxed), and defect/porosity metrics. Physics-based models require EBSD texture measurements to isolate and predict the contribution of each anisotropy source to specific alloys and LPBF processes (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000021).

## 4. Additive Manufacturing Specifically

### Most reported and decision-relevant EBSD outcomes for LPBF

**Crystallographic texture** is identified as the most critical EBSD measurement for AM process qualification, as it is the primary source of elastic and plastic anisotropy in virtually all LPBF metals (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). In LPBF 316L, texture measured by EBSD directly predicts yield-stress and elongation anisotropy and can be used to calibrate crystal plasticity simulations (pqac-00000017). For LPBF Ti-6Al-4V, reconstructed β-phase texture from EBSD reveals ⟨100⟩ fiber texture aligned with the build direction, with alignment disappearing after heat treatment above the α→β transformation temperature (pqac-00000028).

**Columnar vs equiaxed grain morphology** is the second most-reported outcome. Grain elongation in the solidification direction shows periodic variation from melting/remelting patterns; preferentially oriented grains grow at the expense of others, creating wide or bimodal size distributions (pqac-00000006). The NPL guide emphasizes that single mean values of grain size can be meaningless for AM materials without proper context about the distribution and calculation method used (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000025).

**Cell/subgrain structure in AlSi10Mg.** The as-built SLM AlSi10Mg microstructure consists of heterogeneous zones: fine melt-pool cells, coarse melt-pool regions, and heat-affected zones, all composed of primary α-Al cells surrounded by a continuous cellular Si network (pqac-00000049). EBSD combined with XRD tracks cell size evolution through heat treatment and severe plastic deformation, with ECAP reducing grain size from ~1.42 µm to ~0.24 µm after two passes (pqac-00000049). The corrosion resistance of AlSi10Mg improved significantly after ECAP processing, with polarization resistance increasing from ~1.1 kΩ·cm² (as-built) to ~75.5 kΩ·cm² (2 ECAP passes) (pqac-00000050).

**Melt-pool boundary structure and LAGB/HAGB fractions** are widely reported but their isolated contribution to properties is difficult to separate from texture effects. Melt pools primarily affect elongation and ductility rather than strength (pqac-00000009).

**Prior-austenite reconstruction in LPBF steels** is emerging as a high-value technique. In LPBF 17-4 PH steel, five-parameter characterization of intervariant boundaries showed that smaller prior austenite grains improve the grain boundary network by increasing desirable {110} twist boundary plane populations, which are beneficial for controlling hydrogen embrittlement and dislocation plasticity (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047).

## 5. Reproducibility and Measurement-Quality Concerns

The following table summarizes where the literature has documented that acquisition and post-processing choices materially change reported results.

| EBSD Measurement | Key Sensitivity Parameters | Documented Bias/Variability | Relevant Standards | Robustness Rating |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grain size and grain size distribution | Step size/pixel size; grain-definition misorientation threshold; minimum grain size cutoff; treatment of non-indexed points; cleanup; number- vs area-weighting; binning method | In a recrystallized equiaxed alloy, changing GB threshold from 5° to 15° changed mean ECD by **<7%**; in AM datasets, minimum-pixel cutoff and pixel size changed reported mean grain size by about **20%** for number-average metrics; area-weighted metrics were less step-size dependent and better discriminated broad distributions; histogram binning materially changes visual conclusions (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026) | **ISO 13067:2020** for average grain size; **ASTM E2627** commonly referenced for EBSD grain-size practice; NPL guide stresses reporting exact definition/software (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000052) | **Moderate–Robust** |
| Grain morphology / aspect ratio | Step size; segmentation method; ellipse-fitting algorithm; Feret definition; software package; scale range and map visualization choices | Same AM sample analyzed by two vendor packages gave ~**20%** difference in major-axis value after accounting for radius/diameter convention, and inverse aspect-ratio conventions (e.g., 3.3 vs 0.27) can invert interpretation; circularity is highly step-size sensitive because perimeter is discretization-sensitive (pqac-00000027) | No single universal morphology standard inside EBSD software; report definitions/software explicitly; NPL warns defaults differ across vendors (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000052) | **Fragile** |
| Crystallographic texture (ODF, pole figures, texture index) | Sample-axis registration; microscope/EBSD axis calibration; section plane selection; map area representativeness; color scale/IPF choice; reduction/sampling method | Losing AM X-Y-Z orientation can make texture-property interpretation impossible; viewing only one IPF direction can hide strong preferred orientation visible on orthogonal maps; color scales and plotting choices can materially alter apparent heterogeneity even for identical data (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052) | No single texture-only standard cited here; best practice is explicit axis definition and complete reporting of section/sample orientation (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052) | **Moderate** |
| Misorientation distribution and GBCD (including network/connectivity) | Misorientation tolerance; CSL tolerance criterion; cleanup near boundaries; minimum segment length; 2D vs 3D acquisition; stereological assumptions; texture dependence for planar methods | Boundary classification shifts with tolerance choices; coherent vs slightly incoherent Σ3 boundaries can change corrosion/passivation interpretation, with a critical transition reported around **0.4–0.5°** deviation from ideal Σ3 geometry; 2D analyses can miss true connectivity and plane information needed for network conclusions (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039) | No universal consensus standard for 5-parameter GBCD in routine EBSD; reporting of Brandon/CSL criteria and 2D/3D method is essential (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039) | **Moderate–Fragile** |
| KAM, GOS, and GND density | Step size; neighbor order/kernel size; denoising/cleanup; angular resolution/noise floor; boundary exclusion rules; differentiation scheme for GND | KAM is explicitly step-size dependent; local misorientation metrics can be inflated or suppressed by cleanup and kernel definition; GND maps inherit orientation-noise amplification because they require spatial gradients of orientation; interpretation near crack tips and boundaries is especially sensitive to spatial resolution (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000055) | No broadly adopted standard for KAM/GOS/GND reporting; must state step size, kernel, excluded boundaries, and smoothing/cleanup choices (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000025) | **Fragile** |
| Residual elastic strain and stress via HR-EBSD / cross-correlation | Pattern quality; reference pattern choice; detector calibration; surface preparation/edge rounding; strain-free reference assumption; spatial step size; stiffness tensor choice | HR-EBSD offers strain sensitivity of at least **1×10^-4**, but results depend strongly on reference selection and pattern quality; preparation artifacts such as edge rounding can bias crack-tip fields, so papers explicitly note when such errors were avoided (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000055) | No mature universal standard cited here for HR-EBSD stress mapping; full reporting of cross-correlation setup and elastic constants is necessary (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054) | **Fragile** |
| Phase fraction and phase identification | Pattern indexing method; phase library completeness; pseudosymmetry; step size relative to phase size; confidence-index filtering; overlap with second phases | Small or thin second phases are easily missed when step size exceeds feature size; confidence-index filtering can preferentially delete minority-phase pixels; nanoscale phases are often below conventional EBSD spatial resolution and require transmission/HR approaches or correlative methods (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050) | No specific standard cited here beyond normal EBSD reporting practice; phase list/indexing settings must be disclosed | **Moderate–Fragile** |
| Twin and variant analysis | Angular tolerance to ideal twin/variant relation; step size relative to twin thickness/lath width; cleanup that merges thin twins; parent OR assumption | Twin-related conclusions are sensitive to whether boundaries remain coherent versus slightly deviated; thin twins/variants can be lost by coarse step size or cleanup; variant pairing and packet assignment depend on the assumed orientation relationship and reconstruction workflow (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030) | No single standard cited; explicit twin criterion, OR, and pixel/cleanup rules required (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030) | **Fragile** |
| Parent-phase reconstruction (prior-austenite / prior-beta) | Choice/refinement of orientation relationship; graph-clustering parameters; tolerance for child-parent assignment; retained parent fraction; twin handling | Reconstructed parent grains and packet/variant identities can change if OR is not iteratively refined; annealing twins and partial transformations complicate segmentation; therefore property conclusions based on prior-grain size are workflow-sensitive (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000045) | No universal standard; MTEX/related workflows improve transparency but require full disclosure of OR refinement and clustering settings (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000031) | **Fragile** |
| 3D EBSD / serial sectioning derived statistics | Slice thickness; registration accuracy; missing/poor slices; voxel anisotropy; cleanup between slices; segmentation misorientation tolerance | 3D reconstruction quality is highly sensitive to registration and segmentation tolerance; cloud-based reprocessing of TriBeam data showed grain segmentation tolerance can bias reconstructed grain sizes; 3D EBSD is uniquely valuable because 2D can misstate connectivity and true grain shape, but acquisition burden and slice loss remain major limitations (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000056) | No universal 3D EBSD standard cited here; best practice is complete reporting of voxel size, registration, and segmentation parameters (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000056) | **Fragile** |


*Table: This table summarizes which EBSD-derived measurements are most sensitive to acquisition and post-processing choices, and where the literature documents materially different outcomes. It is useful for prioritizing which outputs are suitable for automation and uncertainty quantification first.*

### Key findings on robustness vs fragility

**Most robust:** Area-weighted grain size metrics are the most reproducible EBSD outputs; they reduce dependence on step size and map quality, and better discriminate between samples with different size distributions than number-average metrics (pqac-00000026). Crystallographic texture is moderately robust if sample axis registration is rigorously controlled (pqac-00000051).

**Most fragile:** KAM, GOS, and GND density are explicitly step-size dependent. Local misorientation values scale with step size, and GND density calculations amplify orientation noise because they require spatial gradients (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000055). HR-EBSD strain mapping depends critically on reference pattern selection and surface preparation quality (pqac-00000053). Grain morphology parameters (aspect ratio, ellipticity, circularity) are highly definition-dependent: two commercial software packages analyzing the same AM sample produced ~20% differences in fitted major-axis values and reported inverse aspect-ratio conventions (3.3 vs 0.27), potentially inverting interpretation if not carefully documented (pqac-00000027). 3D EBSD statistics are fragile due to registration, segmentation tolerance, and slice-loss sensitivity (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000044).

**Standards landscape:** ISO 13067:2020 covers average grain size from EBSD, and ASTM E2627 is commonly referenced for EBSD grain-size practice (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000052). No mature universal standards exist for KAM/GOS/GND reporting, HR-EBSD stress mapping, five-parameter GBCD, or grain morphology parameter definitions. The NPL Good Practice Guide (Mingard 2023) specifically warns that different EBSD software packages use different definitions for shape parameters and color scales, and that these choices can materially alter conclusions about sample-to-sample differences (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000052).

## 6. Ranked Shortlist for Automated EBSD Parameter Optimization

The following table presents a prioritized assessment of which EBSD measurements would create the most scientific value if reliably automated with quantified uncertainty, and which are premature targets.

| Priority Tier | EBSD Output | Rationale for Ranking |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 1 Highest Value | Crystallographic texture (ODF, pole figures, texture intensity/index) | Strongest current combination of property payoff, industrial relevance, and modeling demand: directly predicts elastic/plastic anisotropy, modulus, yield-stress directionality, and AM qualification outcomes; is a primary input to CPFEM, ICME, and reduced-order/ML texture representations; reproducibility is moderate if sample axes and plotting conventions are rigorously controlled (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000056) |
| Tier 1 Highest Value | Grain size and grain size distribution | Foundational structure-property descriptor with strong Hall-Petch and hardness relevance and high value for synthetic microstructure generation and statistical volume elements; more reproducible than many advanced metrics if thresholds, minimum grain size, and weighting definition are standardized; ISO 13067 directly supports this as a standardizable target (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000003) |
| Tier 1 Highest Value | Grain morphology / aspect ratio / elongation statistics | Especially high value for AM and CPFEM because columnar-vs-equiaxed morphology and elongation govern anisotropy and representative volume construction; property linkage is meaningful in LPBF, though definitions vary; an optimization tool that also standardizes morphology definitions would solve a real bottleneck (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000052) |
| Tier 2 High Value | Misorientation distribution and grain boundary character distribution (GBCD, CSL fractions, network connectivity) | Strong demonstrated payoff for intergranular corrosion, SCC, corrosion fatigue, and crack-path tortuosity; industrially important in stainless steels and grain-boundary-engineered alloys; however, sensitivity to CSL tolerances, boundary segmentation, and 2D vs 3D assumptions lowers immediate automation readiness versus Tier 1 (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016) |
| Tier 2 High Value | Phase fraction and phase identification | High practical value in multiphase steels, AM alloys, and transformation products; directly relevant to process qualification and mechanical-property partitioning; can be robust when phases are well resolved, but becomes fragile for pseudosymmetry or very fine second phases (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050) |
| Tier 2 High Value | Parent-phase reconstruction plus variant/packet statistics | Very high value in steels and Ti alloys because prior-austenite/prior-β information controls effective grain size, packet hierarchy, toughness, and AM martensitic network interpretation; also increasingly important in LPBF martensitic alloys; kept below Tier 1 because workflow dependence and OR sensitivity remain substantial (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047) |
| Tier 3 Moderate Value | KAM, GOS, and GND density | Extremely popular in the literature and useful for deformation heterogeneity, recrystallization, and fatigue/crack-tip studies, but step-size dependence and noise amplification make them poor first targets unless uncertainty propagation is explicit; best treated as secondary outputs after robust orientation optimization (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000022) |
| Tier 3 Moderate Value | Twin and variant analysis | Important in twinning alloys, martensitic transformations, and grain-boundary-engineered materials; can predict corrosion arrest and local deformation pathways, but requires thin-feature resolution and careful tolerance definitions; narrower industrial breadth than texture or grain size (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000045) |
| Tier 4 Premature/Low Value | Residual elastic strain/stress by HR-EBSD | Scientifically powerful with strong local-mechanics relevance, but currently too fragile, labor-intensive, and under-standardized for broad automated parameter optimization; depends on pattern quality, reference selection, and careful surface preparation, so premature as a general-purpose optimization target (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055) |
| Tier 4 Premature/Low Value | 3D EBSD / serial sectioning derived statistics and five-parameter GBCD | Potentially transformative for true connectivity and grain-boundary-plane statistics, but acquisition burden, registration sensitivity, sparse adoption, and lack of routine standardization make it a poor early automation target except in specialized labs; best as a later-stage extension after robust 2D workflows are solved (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000056) |


*Table: This table ranks EBSD-derived outputs for an automated parameter-optimization tool by expected scientific and industrial value. It prioritizes measurements that combine strong property linkage, reasonable reproducibility, and high demand in AM qualification and ICME/CPFEM workflows.*

### Summary rationale

**Tier 1 (Highest Value)** comprises crystallographic texture, grain size/distribution, and grain morphology/aspect ratio. These three outputs together form the minimal necessary input set for CPFEM, synthetic microstructure generation, and AM process qualification. They have the strongest demonstrated property payoff (anisotropy, Hall-Petch, columnar-vs-equiaxed classification), the highest computational demand, and—critically—their reproducibility weaknesses are addressable through standardized definitions, consistent thresholds, and area-weighted metrics (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000056).

**Tier 2 (High Value)** includes GBCD/misorientation distribution, phase fraction/identification, and parent-phase reconstruction. These outputs have strong property linkage in specific but industrially critical domains (stainless steels for corrosion, multiphase alloys, martensitic steels and Ti alloys), and rising demand in AM qualification. Their lower ranking reflects greater sensitivity to tolerance choices and workflow dependence (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000045).

**Tier 3 (Moderate Value)** covers KAM/GOS/GND density and twin/variant analysis. Although extremely popular in publications, KAM and GND density are poor early-stage automation targets because their inherent step-size dependence means that optimized acquisition parameters will change the absolute values of these metrics, creating a reproducibility paradox unless uncertainty is propagated explicitly (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000022).

**Tier 4 (Premature/Low Value for general-purpose automation)** includes HR-EBSD strain mapping and 3D EBSD statistics. Both are scientifically powerful but too fragile, labor-intensive, and under-standardized for broad automated optimization at present (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000044). They are best pursued as later-stage extensions after robust 2D workflows are established.

In conclusion, an automated EBSD parameter-optimization tool would create the most immediate scientific and industrial value by targeting crystallographic texture, grain size distribution (with area-weighted metrics and explicit threshold reporting per ISO 13067), and standardized grain morphology descriptors as its primary outputs. Misorientation/GBCD and phase identification are strong secondary targets. KAM/GOS/GND, while frequently demanded, should only be automated once their step-size dependence is explicitly addressed through uncertainty quantification. HR-EBSD and 3D EBSD are best reserved for specialized deployment.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents several EBSD-derived quantitative measurements used in analyzing stress corrosion cracking in stainless steels. Key measurements include: (1) Schmid factor in different grains, which appears relevant to understanding slip system activation and plastic deformation; (2) Kernel average misorientation (KAM) maps in radians, indicating local crystallographic distortions; (3) Total geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) density maps in log10 m−2, representing stored dislocations from plastic deformation; (4) Residual elastic strain components around crack tips; (5) Inverse pole figure (IPF) along Z-axis for crystallographic orientation mapping; and (6) High-resolution elastic strain measurements from EBSD patterns. The research demonstrates these measurements in the context of intergranular and transgranular crack propagation, particularly showing correlations between higher Schmid factor grains and crack propagation paths, and stress-induced martensite transformation adjacent to crack paths, suggesting linkages to mechanical response.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses how EBSD measurement parameters affect grain size results. Pixel size significantly influences grain size measurements—a 5 µm pixel size versus 3 µm pixel size eliminates grains that would be analyzed at finer resolution, reducing measured grain size by up to 20% for number average diameter. The effect of pixel size diminishes when using area-weighted diameter calculations. Minimum grain size thresholds (10 pixel vs 5 pixel minimum) also impact results, with smaller minimums including less accurately measured grains. The excerpt emphasizes that pixel size, minimum grain size, and how features are defined must be carefully documented for reproducible comparisons between datasets. Area-weighted calculations reduce dependence on pixel size and minimum length parameters compared to number-based averages.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes EBSD measurements used for synthetic microstructure generation with DREAM.3D. The primary EBSD inputs are: (1) crystallographic orientation information in the form of crystallographic texture, and (2) grain size information from grain size distributions. Specifically, EBSD data is obtained as a 2D orientation image map containing pixel positions and crystallographic orientations. This orientation data is converted to Bunge Euler angles and provided as input to DREAM.3D. Additionally, grain size is computed from pixel position information as equivalent area circle diameter. The 2D grain size data from completely contained grains (not truncated at boundaries) is extracted and then converted to 3D grain size distribution estimates using the Saltykov method. These inputs inform the computation of slip system-level grain sizes and micro-Hall-Petch parameters in the microstructure.

contexts.context: This study correlates grain boundary character measured by EBSD with intergranular corrosion (IGC) resistance in stainless steel. The research uses twin-related domains (TRDs) and grain boundary engineering (GBE) to analyze how GBCD affects IGC. Key findings show that microstructures with larger TRDs containing high densities of Σ3 twin-related grain boundaries demonstrate improved IGC resistance compared to solution-annealed (SA) conditions. The GBE condition exhibited significantly lower degree of sensitization (DOS of 0.25-46.5%) compared to SA (2.7-95%), depending on sensitization time. The study demonstrates that discontinuous networks of corroded boundaries in larger TRDs provide better protection than the highly connected, corroded grain boundary networks in smaller TRDs. Non-twin-related random boundaries at TRD exteriors are most susceptible to IGC attack. This work directly demonstrates the correlation between EBSD-measured grain boundary character and IGC performance through quantitative analysis of TRD statistics and electrochemical testing.

contexts.context: This study investigates how grain boundary engineering (GBE) through thermomechanical processing affects GBCD and corrosion fatigue properties of 316L austenitic stainless steel. GBE enhances grain boundary failure resistance by increasing special boundaries (SBs) and redistributing the grain boundary network. Materials with high frequency of special boundaries (particularly Σ3 boundaries) demonstrate higher resistance to intergranular deterioration due to their higher ordering, closer atomic packing, and lower interface energies. The research shows that GBE can significantly enhance resistance to intergranular corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, and fatigue. However, results reveal a nuanced relationship: while low-energy special boundaries provide strong intergranular corrosion resistance, they are insufficient to resist transgranular fatigue crack propagation. The study uses electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD) through orientation imaging microscopy (OIM) to analyze GBCD. Optimal corrosion fatigue performance was achieved with specific TMP parameters, generating high fractions of special boundaries (approximately 74%).

contexts.context: The excerpt demonstrates that grain boundary character distribution (GBCD), measured through EBSD analysis, directly correlates with corrosion fatigue properties in 316L austenitic stainless steel. Special boundaries (SBs) like Σ3, Σ9, and Σ27 show superior intergranular corrosion resistance compared to random high-angle grain boundaries (RHAGBs), with Σ3 boundaries exhibiting significantly less corrosion depth (210 nm vs 60 nm for RHAGBs). However, while SBs resist intergranular corrosion, they do not effectively block transgranular fatigue crack propagation. The optimal grain boundary engineering condition was found at 45 minutes of annealing with 66% SB content, which achieved both strong corrosion resistance and fatigue resistance, resulting in the longest corrosion fatigue life (3,187 cycles). The study shows that an interrupted network of RHAGBs combined with appropriate SB percentages provides the best balance for corrosion fatigue performance.

contexts.context: This study correlates EBSD-measured grain boundary character with passivation behavior on microcrystalline copper. The research shows that grain boundaries classified as the same CSL type by EBSD exhibit varying passivation efficiency, indicating that local GB structure variations affect corrosion reactivity. Random-type high-angle boundaries demonstrate lower passivation efficiency and higher susceptibility to intergranular attack compared to CSL boundaries. The deviation angle of the GB plane from ideal coherent geometry influences local reactivity: larger deviations (higher incoherence) correlate with lower passivation efficiency and thicker passive films, while smaller deviations correlate with better passivation efficiency. The study demonstrates that refined EBSD analysis of misorientation and deviation angles provides insight into local GB structure heterogeneity that explains variable corrosion behavior at different sites along the same boundary.

contexts.context: This study combines ECSTM (Electrochemical Scanning Tunneling Microscopy) and EBSD analysis to examine relationships between grain boundary character and passivation efficiency in microcrystalline copper. The research demonstrates that grain boundary type significantly affects corrosion behavior. Coherent twin boundaries (Σ3 CSL) with low deviation angles (≤0.3°) show higher passivation efficiency with thinner passive films on adjacent grains, while high angle random boundaries exhibit less efficient passivation. A critical transition in passivation efficiency occurs at deviation angles of 0.4-0.5° from perfect geometry in Σ3 boundaries. This transition correlates with the presence and density of misfit dislocations (steps) in the boundary plane. The study reveals that increasing dislocation density becomes more detrimental for passivation efficiency than for resistance to active dissolution, suggesting that grain boundary fine structure plays a crucial role in determining localized corrosion susceptibility.

contexts.context: The excerpt demonstrates that GBCD and grain boundary engineering measured by EBSD correlate significantly with stress corrosion cracking (SCC) resistance. The study shows that high fractions of CSL (coincident site lattice) boundaries achieved through grain boundary engineering improve mechanical properties and SCC resistance in 304 stainless steel tested in high-temperature water. EBSD analysis reveals that the connectivity and network configuration of non-twin boundaries is crucial for preventing intergranular SCC propagation. The GBE-treated specimen exhibited fewer secondary cracks and greater resistance to crack initiation and propagation compared to conventional material. The disruption of continuous non-twin boundary pathways through increased CSL boundaries forces SCC propagation to take longer, more tortuous routes through the material, thereby enhancing overall corrosion cracking resistance.

contexts.context: The excerpt explains the fundamental link between crystallographic texture (measured via EBSD using pole figures and inverse pole figure grain maps) and mechanical anisotropy in metals. When polycrystalline materials develop crystallographic texture—where specific crystal orientations occur at higher frequencies than random distributions—the macroscopic mechanical properties inherit the anisotropic characteristics of individual crystals. The texture is characterized by crystal orientation components and their intensity (measured in multiples of uniform distribution). The excerpt emphasizes that the main source of elastic anisotropy in additive metals is crystallographic texture, with the macroscopic anisotropy determined by the single crystal elastic anisotropy combined with the texture component(s) and intensity. Voigt, Ruess, and Hill theories provide bounds and predictions for relating polycrystalline elastic anisotropy to single crystal properties. The excerpt notes that texture affects Young's modulus measurements at different sample orientations, which can be predicted from measured single crystal elastic constants.

Texture causes plastic anisotropy because slip and other deformation mechanisms depend on crystal plane orientation relative to the loading axis. The document presents two LPBF 316L stainless steel cases: one with moderate texture showing 15% strength variation (X: 581 MPa vs Z: 506-514 MPa yield), and another with extreme Goss texture (21 m.u.d.) showing 30% strength difference between (111) and (100) directions. # Summary

This NPL Good Practice Guide (No. 152) addresses EBSD analysis of additively manufactured materials. The document emphasizes that EBSD mapping of polished AM sections reveals "the size, shape and orientation of the grains and their distribution," which can be "related to the physical properties of the components produced." 

A key theme is **measurement reproducibility and standardization**: the guide stresses that "the wrong choice of EBSD acquisition conditions or parameters to plot can result in erroneous conclusions, based on noisy or restricted...data sets." It highlights critical concerns including "acquisition conditions," parameter selection, and proper reporting to "enable comparison between different locations in the component" and "between parts, suggesting variation [in] manufacturing conditions." The guide targets AM producers and users, emphasizing the need for careful choices in mapping representative areas, grain size measurement calculation methods, and visualization approaches to avoid "misleading comparisons." The document uses Ni-base superalloy AM examples to illustrate how spatial variation and microstructural features can be reliably characterized and compared.
contexts.question:
Which quantitative microstructural outcomes and measurements derivable from EBSD (electron backscatter diffraction) are currently of highest scientific and industrial importance in materials science, and why?

Provide a prioritized, evidence-backed survey covering:

1. WHICH EBSD-DERIVED QUANTITIES MATTER MOST NOW. Assess the current importance, demand, and research activity for each of: grain size and grain size distribution; grain morphology/aspect ratio; crystallographic texture (ODF, pole figures, texture index) ; misorientation distribution and grain boundary character distribution (GBCD, including the five-parameter grain boundary character distribution and grain boundary network/connectivity analysis); kernel average misorientation (KAM), grain orientation spread (GOS), and geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) density; residual elastic strain and stress via high-resolution EBSD (HR-EBSD / cross-correlation); phase fraction and phase identification including small or nanoscale second phases; twin and variant analysis; parent-phase (prior-austenite / prior-beta) reconstruction; and 3D EBSD / serial sectioning derived statistics.

2. STRUCTURE-PROPERTY LINKAGE. For each quantity above, what is the evidence that it predicts or correlates with engineering properties (yield strength and Hall-Petch behaviour, ductility, anisotropy, fatigue crack initiation and short-crack growth, creep, fracture toughness, corrosion and stress-corrosion cracking, magnetic and electrical properties)? Which EBSD measurements have the strongest demonstrated property payoff, and which are most often reported but weakly linked to properties?

3. EMERGING AND HIGH-GROWTH USES (roughly 2020-2026). Which EBSD-derived measurements are in rising demand as inputs to: ICME and integrated computational materials engineering; crystal plasticity finite element modelling (CPFEM) and micromechanical simulation; synthetic microstructure generation and statistical volume elements; machine learning surrogate models and microstructure-property regression; digital twins; and qualification of additively manufactured metals? Which quantities are the actual bottleneck for these workflows?

4. ADDITIVE MANUFACTURING SPECIFICALLY. For laser powder bed fusion metals (particularly Al-Si alloys such as AlSi10Mg, but also Ti-6Al-4V, IN718, 316L), which EBSD outcomes are most reported and most decision-relevant for process qualification and part certification (columnar vs equiaxed grain morphology, solidification texture and its anisotropy consequences, melt-pool boundary structure, cell/subgrain structure, low-angle vs high-angle boundary fractions, residual strain)?

5. REPRODUCIBILITY AND MEASUREMENT-QUALITY CONCERNS. Which of these EBSD-derived measurements are known to be most sensitive to acquisition and post-processing choices (step size, indexing method and settings, cleanup/noise-reduction, misorientation threshold, minimum grain size, confidence-index filtering), and where has the literature documented that these choices materially change the reported result or bias downstream conclusions? Which measurements are considered robust and which are considered fragile or under-standardized (including relevant standards such as ASTM E2627 and ISO 13067)?

Conclude with a ranked shortlist: if an automated EBSD parameter-optimization tool could reliably deliver a small number of these measurements with quantified uncertainty and reproducibility, which measurements would create the most scientific value, and which would be premature or low-value targets? Give explicit citations throughout.

# Summary

This excerpt addresses grain size characterization in metallic alloys using microscopy and post-processing techniques. Key points include:

**Primary Finding:** "Grain Size (GS), or more generally the Grain Size Distribution (GSD), is one of the main microstructural characteristics of a metallic alloy, in particular because it is determinant for mechanical properties." The authors emphasize that "working directly with GSD provides more information, in particular regarding the spread around MGS or the description of multimodal microstructures."

**EBSD Capabilities:** EBSD "can provide precise GSD information based on crystallographic orientations even considering ultrafine-grained microstructures" and enables quantification of grain boundaries and local misorientation via "Kernel Average Misorientation (KAM)" that provides insight into "Geometrically Necessary Dislocations (GND) densities."

**Measurement Comparison:** The study compares EBSD results with image analysis from optical and backscattered electron (BSE) micrographs, examining "the effect of data processing parameters on grain size results." For coarse-grained materials, "Optical Microscopy (OM) or BackScattered Electron (BSE) imaging...enable larger view fields and shorter acquisition times compared to EBSD."

**Standardization Context:** Multiple grain size definitions are discussed including "mean intercept length," "equivalent circle diameter," and "ASTM grain size."

# Summary

This excerpt examines **grain size (GS) measurement reproducibility and sensitivity** across EBSD and optical microscopy techniques. Key findings:

**Measurement Sensitivity:**
- EBSD misorientation angle threshold (5°, 10°, or 15°) materially affects results: lower thresholds detect more grains, decreasing mean grain size (MGS); "ECD variation remains under 7%" within this range (Table 2, Fig. 10).
- Different MGS definitions (Eq. 2–11) yield varying values: individual grain data gave 35.8–40.5 μm; counting/intercept methods overestimated by ~10%.

**Post-Processing Sensitivity:**
- Mean filter parameter (Rm) critically influences grain boundary (GB) detection; Rm = 6–9 px optimal; Rm = 15 px introduced "detrimental artefacts."
- Polarized light microscopy (PL-OM) required "3 to 4 images" for stable MGS estimates.

**Comparative Validation:**
For homogeneous equiaxed microstructure (Zy-4): EBSD and PL-OM gave "similar MGS results," supporting measurement robustness in this case.

The work demonstrates that grain size—foundational to materials science—exhibits **significant parameter-dependent variability** requiring standardization.

# Summary

This excerpt describes EBSD and comparative microstructural characterization techniques for grain size determination in Zircaloy-4 and 304L stainless steel. 

**EBSD Acquisition Parameters:** Step sizes of 0.3 μm (Zy-4) and 1 μm (304L) were used with Bruker Quantax and Oxford Instruments detectors. Non-indexed points (<2% at grain boundaries) were ignored, and isolated indexed points were filtered using minimum grain size thresholds of 1.5 μm and 5 μm respectively, corresponding to 5-pixel minimums.

**Key EBSD-Derived Measurements Compared:** The study benchmarks EBSD against optical metallography (OM) and backscattered electron (BSE) imaging for grain size distribution (GSD) and mean grain size (MGS) evaluation, using mean linear intercept as a reference metric.

**Grain Boundary Detection:** The excerpt describes automated edge-detection methodology using Sobel filters and watershed transforms on multi-contrast image sets to extract grain boundaries and morphological properties, emphasizing sensitivity to acquisition parameters (tilt angle, polarization angle) and post-processing choices.

The work directly addresses reproducibility concerns tied to acquisition settings and cleanup procedures affecting reported grain metrics.

# Summary

This excerpt addresses **reproducibility and measurement-quality concerns** in EBSD-derived grain morphology quantification, specifically grain size and aspect ratio measurements.

The text emphasizes that **definition standardization is critical**: grain morphology metrics (Feret diameters, ellipse-fitted axes, aspect ratio, ellipticity, circularity) lack agreed definitions across software vendors. Table 2 demonstrates this concretely—analyzing >4000 grains from the same sample yielded major axis values differing by ~20% and aspect ratios reported as reciprocals (3.3 vs 0.27) between two software packages, even after accounting for diameter vs. radius differences.

Key fragilities identified include:
- **Ellipse fitting methods** (least squares, covariance, Feret-based) "will produce different results" 
- **Aspect ratio definitions** (major/minor vs. minor/major) invert outcomes
- **Circularity calculations** are "significantly" affected by step size/pixel resolution
- **Colour scale visualization** choices ("flat zones," undefined ranges, perceptual non-linearity) obscure or misrepresent spatial variation

The section concludes that if software and definitions are not explicitly reported, dataset comparison is impossible, indicating aspect ratio and grain morphology measures are **fragile and under-standardized** despite widespread use.
contexts.question:
Which quantitative microstructural outcomes and measurements derivable from EBSD (electron backscatter diffraction) are currently of highest scientific and industrial importance in materials science, and why?

Provide a prioritized, evidence-backed survey covering:

1. WHICH EBSD-DERIVED QUANTITIES MATTER MOST NOW. Assess the current importance, demand, and research activity for each of: grain size and grain size distribution; grain morphology/aspect ratio; crystallographic texture (ODF, pole figures, texture index) ; misorientation distribution and grain boundary character distribution (GBCD, including the five-parameter grain boundary character distribution and grain boundary network/connectivity analysis); kernel average misorientation (KAM), grain orientation spread (GOS), and geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) density; residual elastic strain and stress via high-resolution EBSD (HR-EBSD / cross-correlation); phase fraction and phase identification including small or nanoscale second phases; twin and variant analysis; parent-phase (prior-austenite / prior-beta) reconstruction; and 3D EBSD / serial sectioning derived statistics.

2. STRUCTURE-PROPERTY LINKAGE. For each quantity above, what is the evidence that it predicts or correlates with engineering properties (yield strength and Hall-Petch behaviour, ductility, anisotropy, fatigue crack initiation and short-crack growth, creep, fracture toughness, corrosion and stress-corrosion cracking, magnetic and electrical properties)? Which EBSD measurements have the strongest demonstrated property payoff, and which are most often reported but weakly linked to properties?

3. EMERGING AND HIGH-GROWTH USES (roughly 2020-2026). Which EBSD-derived measurements are in rising demand as inputs to: ICME and integrated computational materials engineering; crystal plasticity finite element modelling (CPFEM) and micromechanical simulation; synthetic microstructure generation and statistical volume elements; machine learning surrogate models and microstructure-property regression; digital twins; and qualification of additively manufactured metals? Which quantities are the actual bottleneck for these workflows?

4. ADDITIVE MANUFACTURING SPECIFICALLY. For laser powder bed fusion metals (particularly Al-Si alloys such as AlSi10Mg, but also Ti-6Al-4V, IN718, 316L), which EBSD outcomes are most reported and most decision-relevant for process qualification and part certification (columnar vs equiaxed grain morphology, solidification texture and its anisotropy consequences, melt-pool boundary structure, cell/subgrain structure, low-angle vs high-angle boundary fractions, residual strain)?

5. REPRODUCIBILITY AND MEASUREMENT-QUALITY CONCERNS. Which of these EBSD-derived measurements are known to be most sensitive to acquisition and post-processing choices (step size, indexing method and settings, cleanup/noise-reduction, misorientation threshold, minimum grain size, confidence-index filtering), and where has the literature documented that these choices materially change the reported result or bias downstream conclusions? Which measurements are considered robust and which are considered fragile or under-standardized (including relevant standards such as ASTM E2627 and ISO 13067)?

Conclude with a ranked shortlist: if an automated EBSD parameter-optimization tool could reliably deliver a small number of these measurements with quantified uncertainty and reproducibility, which measurements would create the most scientific value, and which would be premature or low-value targets? Give explicit citations throughout.

# Summary

The excerpt addresses grain size measurement methodology and reproducibility challenges in EBSD analysis. Key findings:

**Measurement Sensitivity:** Three different grain size calculation methods (number average diameter, mean area diameter, area-weighted diameter) yield substantially different results. For Sample 1, values ranged from 23.3–44.5 µm; for Sample 2, from 29.4–85.7 µm. "The effect of pixel size is much reduced if the mean area diameter is calculated," but area-weighted methods show 40% differences between samples.

**Binning and Representation Effects:** Histogram binning choices materially alter reported distributions. "Log scale binning increases the number of ranges at the lower size end and reduces them at larger values, shifting the distribution down and to the right," changing visual interpretation of the same data.

**Minimum Grain Size Dependency:** Changing minimum grain size thresholds (10 pixels vs. 5 pixels) reduced Sample 1's number average by 20%, demonstrating sensitivity to post-processing parameters.

**Parameter Definition Ambiguity:** For elongated grains, multiple metrics exist (linear intercepts, Feret diameters, ellipse fitting, aspect ratios), yet "a very significant factor to beware of when publishing the data...is understanding exactly how each feature is defined," indicating standardization gaps.

The excerpt emphasizes that grain size—EBSD's most fundamental metric—is fragile regarding acquisition and analysis choices.

contexts.context: This paper describes a framework for parent grain reconstruction and variant analysis in MTEX, an open-source crystallographic toolbox. Parent grain reconstruction enables analysis of original microstructures prior to phase transformation and allows variant analysis for fully transformed microstructures. The paper discusses applications in martensitic steel, titanium alloys, and transformation-induced plasticity steel. Regarding material properties, the authors note that martensitic transformation increases mechanical strength through Hall-Petch hardening via hierarchical subdivision of parent grains into child domains, reducing effective grain size. Additional strengthening can be achieved through interstitial solid solution strengthening and increased dislocation density from plastic strain accommodating volume mismatch between parent and child phases. However, the excerpt does not directly address twin analysis or provide specific details on how these techniques link to toughness properties.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the theoretical foundations and computational methods for parent grain reconstruction from transformed microstructures. Parent grain reconstruction determines parent orientations by identifying multiple unique and adjacent child grains that originated from the same parent via different symmetry operations, since a single child orientation cannot uniquely determine parent orientation due to crystal symmetry. The paper discusses orientation relationships (ORs) between parent and child phases, how symmetry operators generate multiple orientation variants, and grain-level computational approaches implemented in MTEX software. It covers growth algorithms for partially transformed microstructures (where retained parent phase acts as nuclei) and nucleation algorithms for fully transformed microstructures. The difficulty of reconstruction depends on the number of possible orientation variants—more variants require identification of more adjacent child grains, making αᇱ-to-γ reconstruction in martensitic steels more challenging than α-to-β in Ti alloys.

contexts.context: The excerpt demonstrates that HR-KAM (kernel average misorientation) and GND (geometrically necessary dislocation) density measurements effectively characterize plastic deformation associated with stress corrosion crack propagation in stainless steel. Higher HR-KAM values concentrate at crack edges and grain boundaries ahead of crack tips, indicating localized plastic deformation. GND density maps show similar patterns, with elevated values at crack edges, grain boundaries, and triple points, demonstrating substantial plastic deformation in these regions. contexts.context: EBSD is used in this fatigue study to characterize crystallographic features of grains containing fatigue cracks. Post-experiment, specimen surfaces were polished and analyzed using a field emission SEM equipped with an EBSD detector at step-sizes of 0.15-0.3 µm. Custom procedures estimated crystallographic features including Schmid factor and geometric compatibility factor. Slip traces from different slip systems were calculated and compared directly to crack paths to identify the activated primary slip system and confirm the crystallographic nature of crack behavior. The study analyzed 596 crack segments and 180 cracked grain boundaries. Results showed cracks initiated preferentially in grains with high Schmid factor on prismatic slip systems, and crystal orientations were mapped on inverse pole figures relative to the loading direction. This approach enabled correlation between specific crystallographic orientations, Schmid factors, and actual crack initiation and propagation paths.

contexts.context: EBSD (Electron Backscatter Diffraction) is employed to systematically investigate the influence of microstructure on fatigue crack initiation and propagation in Ti-6Al-4V. The crystallographic orientation, measured via EBSD, determines crack initiation sites, which occur on prismatic slip planes with high Schmid factors in both primary α grains and lamellar colonies. The Schmid factor quantifies the plastic strain activity and helps predict which slip systems are activated. At grain boundaries, crack deflection is governed by two competing factors: the geometric compatibility factor (strain compatibility at the interface) and the Schmid factor in neighboring grains. The elastic anisotropy of grains influences which factor dominates crack propagation—either high Schmid factor slip systems or high geometric compatibility factor slip systems. EBSD analysis, combined with KAM (Kernel Average Misorientation) mapping, reveals that crack paths remain planar and crystallographic, driven by mode II shear mechanisms, and are sensitive to microstructural features including grain size and orientation relationships.

contexts.context: This study uses post-mortem electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD) analyses combined with in situ optical microscopy to investigate fatigue crack initiation and short crack propagation in rolled Ti-6Al-4V alloy. contexts.context: This excerpt describes 3D EBSD serial sectioning methodology for analyzing grain boundary character distribution in yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ). The technique uses dual beam-focused ion beam SEM to map microstructure and identify triple junctions across parallel layers. The five-parameter grain boundary character distribution represents relative grain boundary areas as a function of crystallographic parameters. Grain boundary plane orientations are calculated from cross products of tangent vectors and triple line vectors. The study relates grain boundary crystallography to energy: (100) twist boundaries exhibit greater relative areas and lower relative energies compared to other boundary types. contexts.context: This study characterizes grain boundary plane distributions in AZ31 Mg alloy using five-parameter grain boundary analysis. The research examines the relationship between grain boundary plane orientations and grain boundary energy. According to established theory, grain boundary areas are inversely correlated with grain boundary energy, with frequently observed boundaries having the smallest energy. The interplanar spacing model predicts that planes with large interplanar spacings have lower energy due to being flatter, smoother, with fewer broken bonds. However, in the AZ31 Mg alloy studied, this inverse relationship does not hold: prismatic planes {hki0} with relatively small interplanar spacings (0.43-1.86 Å) are most frequently observed, while the basal plane (0001) with the largest interplanar spacing (2.6 Å) shows minimum population. The grain boundary plane distribution exhibits relatively weak anisotropy with only 7% deviation from random distribution, with a preference for prismatic planes.

contexts.context: This excerpt discusses grain boundary characterization in yttria-stabilized zirconia using five-parameter analysis. The methodology involves computing grain boundary areas and energies at specific points in five-dimensional space using kernel density approximation, with apertures of 6° misorientation and 7° grain boundary plane inclination. The text demonstrates the relationship between grain boundary plane orientations and energy: grain boundary energy shows significant anisotropy across different boundary types in 5D space. contexts.context: The five-parameter grain boundary character distribution (GBCD) characterizes olivine grain boundaries using five parameters: three parameters describing disorientation (axis and angle) and two parameters describing grain boundary plane distribution (GBPD)—one radial and one azimuthal angle (Φ and θ). Recent EBSD technology enables statistical extraction of these parameters across large datasets (10^4-10^5 grain boundaries). The GBCD encompasses grain boundary geometry-energy relationships: particular grain boundary plane orientations at constant disorientation angles are more energetically favorable than others. Grain boundary energy minimization is primarily controlled by surface energy reduction of individual grains in contact rather than adaptation of special atomic configurations. Two main 3D EBSD measurement approaches exist: serial sectioning and stereological analysis of 2D orientation maps, though stereology requires materials without significant orientation texture.

## Summary

This excerpt describes EBSD methodology applied to an AlSi10Mg alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) and severe plastic deformation (ECAP). 

**EBSD Acquisition Details:**
Step sizes varied: "0.3 µm for heat-treated (S2), 0.09 µm for 1 ECAP (S2-1), and 0.06 µm for 2 ECAP (S2-2) samples." Data cleaning involved "neighbor orientation correlation data cleaning process (level 4)" followed by "grain confidence index standardization cleanup with a grain tolerance angle threshold of 2°" and "coincidence index filter of 0.05."

**Microstructural Features Characterized:**
The SLM as-built microstructure exhibited heterogeneous zones: "'MP fine' zone was composed of fine primary α-Al cells (darker gray) surrounded by a continuous cellular Si network (lighter white). The 'MP coarse' zone consisted of a coarser Si network." The XZ plane showed "semicircular (fish-scale) patterns along the Z-direction."

**Limitation:** The excerpt provides practical EBSD methodology but does not address the broader question of which EBSD-derived quantities (grain size, texture, misorientation, KAM, GND density, strain, etc.) are of highest scientific/industrial importance or their structure-property linkages.
contexts.question:
Which quantitative microstructural outcomes and measurements derivable from EBSD (electron backscatter diffraction) are currently of highest scientific and industrial importance in materials science, and why?

Provide a prioritized, evidence-backed survey covering:

1. WHICH EBSD-DERIVED QUANTITIES MATTER MOST NOW. Assess the current importance, demand, and research activity for each of: grain size and grain size distribution; grain morphology/aspect ratio; crystallographic texture (ODF, pole figures, texture index) ; misorientation distribution and grain boundary character distribution (GBCD, including the five-parameter grain boundary character distribution and grain boundary network/connectivity analysis); kernel average misorientation (KAM), grain orientation spread (GOS), and geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) density; residual elastic strain and stress via high-resolution EBSD (HR-EBSD / cross-correlation); phase fraction and phase identification including small or nanoscale second phases; twin and variant analysis; parent-phase (prior-austenite / prior-beta) reconstruction; and 3D EBSD / serial sectioning derived statistics.

2. STRUCTURE-PROPERTY LINKAGE. For each quantity above, what is the evidence that it predicts or correlates with engineering properties (yield strength and Hall-Petch behaviour, ductility, anisotropy, fatigue crack initiation and short-crack growth, creep, fracture toughness, corrosion and stress-corrosion cracking, magnetic and electrical properties)? Which EBSD measurements have the strongest demonstrated property payoff, and which are most often reported but weakly linked to properties?

3. EMERGING AND HIGH-GROWTH USES (roughly 2020-2026). Which EBSD-derived measurements are in rising demand as inputs to: ICME and integrated computational materials engineering; crystal plasticity finite element modelling (CPFEM) and micromechanical simulation; synthetic microstructure generation and statistical volume elements; machine learning surrogate models and microstructure-property regression; digital twins; and qualification of additively manufactured metals? Which quantities are the actual bottleneck for these workflows?

4. ADDITIVE MANUFACTURING SPECIFICALLY. For laser powder bed fusion metals (particularly Al-Si alloys such as AlSi10Mg, but also Ti-6Al-4V, IN718, 316L), which EBSD outcomes are most reported and most decision-relevant for process qualification and part certification (columnar vs equiaxed grain morphology, solidification texture and its anisotropy consequences, melt-pool boundary structure, cell/subgrain structure, low-angle vs high-angle boundary fractions, residual strain)?

5. REPRODUCIBILITY AND MEASUREMENT-QUALITY CONCERNS. Which of these EBSD-derived measurements are known to be most sensitive to acquisition and post-processing choices (step size, indexing method and settings, cleanup/noise-reduction, misorientation threshold, minimum grain size, confidence-index filtering), and where has the literature documented that these choices materially change the reported result or bias downstream conclusions? Which measurements are considered robust and which are considered fragile or under-standardized (including relevant standards such as ASTM E2627 and ISO 13067)?

Conclude with a ranked shortlist: if an automated EBSD parameter-optimization tool could reliably deliver a small number of these measurements with quantified uncertainty and reproducibility, which measurements would create the most scientific value, and which would be premature or low-value targets? Give explicit citations throughout.

## Summary

This excerpt examines AlSi10Mg alloy microstructure and corrosion behavior using EBSD and XRD analysis across multiple processing conditions (as-built S0, heat-treated S2, and ECAP-processed S2-1 and S2-2).

**Crystallographic texture** is documented via (111) pole figures showing evolution from initial state through ECAP passes. After one ECAP pass, a "strong shear A∗₁A∗₂ {111}<112> texture component with a maximum intensity of ~4.6 mr (multiply random)" emerged; further deformation strengthened this component and introduced "B B {112}<110> texture component."

**Microstructural changes** affected corrosion resistance: heat treatment depleted Si solid solution from 1.1 at% to 0.3 at%, altering Si precipitate morphology. ECAP processing extended Si solubility to 2.2 at% after one pass, then depleted it to 0.7 at% after two passes via "dynamic precipitation of supersaturated Si."

**Structure-property linkage** is demonstrated through corrosion data: ECAP-processed samples showed dramatically improved corrosion resistance with corrosion current density icorr decreasing from 7.3–18.5 µA/cm² (as-built/heat-treated) to 0.2–0.3 µA/cm² (ECAP samples), and polarization resistance Rp increasing to 60.6–75.5 kΩ·cm².
